a: another one besides the first famine
t: The third "she is my sister" story
p: Abraham did this twice (12:10–20; 20:1–18). Now Isaac repeats it, in the same town, with the same king's name.
b: Genesis tells three stories in which a patriarch passes off his wife as his sister: Abraham in Egypt (12:10–20), Abraham in Gerar (20:1–18), and Isaac here. The narrator knows the reader remembers the first famine. Traditional readers take these as three real events: the son learns his father's habits, good and bad. Many critical scholars see one old story told in three versions from different sources, often assigning 12 and 26 to J (the source that names God "the LORD") and 20 to E (the source that prefers "God"); see the topic on the Pentateuch's sources. Literary readers note how each retelling changes: here no one takes Rebekah, and God does not have to intervene with a dream or a plague.

a: Abimelech king of the Philistines
t: Philistines in the time of Isaac?
p: The Philistines settled the coast around 1175 BC, long after any date for Isaac. How do we explain the name?
b: Egyptian records of Ramesses III (Medinet Habu, early 1100s BC) describe the arrival of "Sea Peoples," among them the Peleset, who settled the southern coast of Canaan. Most scholars therefore see "Philistines" here as an anachronism: a later writer used the name his readers knew for the people of that region. Conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen suggest earlier Aegean traders lived in the area and were called by the later name, as we say "Native Americans" of people before the name existed. "Abimelech" ("my father is king") may also be a royal title rather than one man: Psalm 34's heading calls King Achish of Gath "Abimelech." Either way this cannot be the same young king of chapter 20, at least sixty years earlier and perhaps nearly a hundred (25:26; 26:34), unless he lived very long.

a: Do not go down to Egypt
p: Abraham went to Egypt in a famine; Isaac is told to stay. He is the only patriarch who never leaves Canaan.
b: Abraham went down to Egypt in his famine (12:10), and Jacob will go down in his (46:3–4). Isaac alone is told to stay, and he never leaves the land. Abraham had already insisted that his son must not be taken back to Mesopotamia (24:6, 8). Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, gives the reason: Isaac had been laid on the altar on Mount Moriah, so he was like a whole burnt offering, and "outside the land is not worthy of you." Modern readers notice a simpler point: the promise of the land is tested by staying in it when it is hungry.

a: will bless themselves by your offspring
p: The Hebrew form here usually means "bless themselves," not "be blessed." The difference matters for Acts and Galatians.
b: God's promise that the nations will be blessed through Abraham's line comes five times (12:3; 18:18; 22:18; 26:4; 28:14). Twice the verb is passive ("be blessed"); here and in 22:18 it is reflexive (hitbarekhu), which normally means "bless themselves": people will say "May God make you like Isaac's offspring," using the formula of 48:20. Many scholars hold that the meanings overlap: a family used as the model blessing is also the channel of blessing. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, used a passive throughout, and the New Testament quotes it that way (Acts 3:25; Galatians 3:8). Paul also builds on the singular noun "offspring" (Galatians 3:16), which he reads as pointing to Christ.

a: my commands, my rules and my laws
t: Abraham kept the Torah before Sinai?
p: These four words for God's law come straight out of Deuteronomy. The rabbis drew a famous conclusion.
b: "Charge, commands, decrees and teachings" (mishmarti, mitsvotai, chuqqotai, torotai) is the vocabulary of the laws of Moses (Deuteronomy 11:1). The Mishnah concludes that "Abraham our father kept the whole Torah before it was given" (Kiddushin 4:14), and the Talmud says he even kept the later rabbinic rules (Yoma 28b). Ramban adds that the patriarchs kept the commandments only in the land of Israel (see 29:28). Christian readers have stressed instead that Abraham was counted righteous by faith before the law (15:6; Romans 4:13; Galatians 3:17), and read the verse as describing a life of trust and obedience. Critical scholars see the hand of an editor trained in Deuteronomy's language.

a: She is my sister
p: Sarah was Abraham's half sister (20:12). Rebekah is only Isaac's kinswoman, his cousin's daughter.
b: When Abraham said "she is my sister," he could claim a half-truth (20:12). Isaac has less to go on: Hebrew achot can mean "kinswoman" (her own family calls her "our sister," 24:60), but Rebekah is the daughter of his cousin Bethuel (24:15), not his sister. In 1963 E. A. Speiser argued that tablets from Nuzi, a Hurrian town in northern Iraq (1400s BC), showed a custom of "wife-sister" marriage that gave a wife higher status, and that Genesis preserved a garbled memory of it. Later study (Samuel Greengus, 1975) showed the Nuzi documents do not say this, and the theory is now generally abandoned. The stories are best read as what they seem: a frightened man protecting himself at his wife's expense.

a: Isaac playing with Rebekah his wife
p: The verb is a pun on Isaac's name, "he laughs." Here it means loving play between husband and wife.
b: Isaac's name, Yitschaq, means "he laughs" (17:17; 18:12; 21:6). The verb here is the same root: metsacheq, "laughing, playing." A reader could almost say that Isaac was "isaacing" with Rebekah. The context shows it was the kind of play only a husband and wife share, and the king knew at once what he had seen. The same verb carries other shades in other places: mocking (21:9), sexual insult (39:14, 17), and revelry (Exodus 32:6).
orig: מְצַחֵק (metsacheq), from the root of יִצְחָק (Yitschaq)

a: you would have brought guilt on us
t: The foreign king has the higher morals
p: As in chapters 12 and 20, the outsider guards marriage better than the man of God.
b: In all three wife-sister stories the foreign ruler is shocked, and he is right to be. Egyptian and Ugaritic texts call adultery "the great sin," the phrase Abimelech used in 20:9. The Hebrew 'asham, "guilt," is the word later used for the guilt offering (Leviticus 5:14–19). Abimelech then puts the couple under royal protection on pain of death. Genesis does not flatter its heroes: the chosen family is not chosen because it behaves better than everyone else.

a: a hundred times what he sowed
p: Ancient harvests yielded far less. A hundredfold is a sign of blessing, and Jesus' parable of the sower echoes it.
b: Isaac becomes a farmer as well as a herdsman, and his first crop yields a hundred times what he sowed. Ancient records suggest normal yields far below that, so the narrator adds at once: "The LORD blessed him." The picture is taken up in Jesus' parable of the sower, where seed in good soil gives a crop, "one thirty times as much, another sixty, another a hundred" (Mark 4:8). For a different reading in the Greek, see the textual note.

a: stopped up and filled with dirt
t: Wells as life and as weapons
p: In the dry Negev a well was wealth. Filling one in was an act of war.
b: Around Gerar and Beersheba the rain is light and unreliable, and herds depend on wells dug down to groundwater. To stop a well was to drive a rival away. Armies did the same in war (2 Kings 3:19, 25). Isaac's response is striking: he does not fight but digs again, and when he is challenged he moves on. Many readers see in him the quietest of the patriarchs, a man who receives more than he takes.

a: Sitnah
p: The well's name comes from the same root as Satan, "accuser" or "opponent."
b: Esek means "Quarrel" and Sitnah means "Hostility" or "Accusation." Sitnah comes from the root s-t-n, "to oppose, accuse," the same root as satan, used of a human opponent (1 Kings 11:14), of the LORD's angel standing in Balaam's way (Numbers 22:22), and of the accuser in Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3. Here it is just a name for a well people fought over. Rehoboth, the third well, means "Wide Spaces." The names tell the story in three words: quarrel, hostility, room.

a: Rehoboth
p: Often placed at Ruheibeh, southwest of Beersheba, though the match is uncertain.
b: The name survives, perhaps, in the ruins of Ruheibeh (Rehovot ba-Negev), about 20 miles southwest of Beersheba, where there are old wells. The identification is traditional and possible but not proven. It is not the Rehoboth of 10:11 in Assyria or the "Rehoboth on the River" of 36:37. The modern Israeli city of Rehovot took its name from this verse.

a: for the sake of Abraham my servant
p: God blesses Isaac because of Abraham. Jewish tradition calls this zekhut avot, the merit of the fathers.
b: This is the only time in Genesis that God appears to Isaac at night, and the promise rests on Abraham: "for the sake of Abraham my servant." Moses later prays the same way after the golden calf (Exodus 32:13), and David's line is spared "because of David my servant" (1 Kings 11:13). Jewish tradition built on this the idea of zekhut avot, the merit of the fathers, which is still invoked in the daily Amidah prayer ("who remembers the loving deeds of the fathers"). Christians read the same pattern as blessing that comes through another's faithfulness, fulfilled in Christ.

a: let us make a covenant with you
p: Abraham made a treaty with Abimelech and Phicol at Beersheba too (21:22–34). Is this one event or two?
b: Chapter 21 tells of Abraham, Abimelech and Phicol swearing an oath over a disputed well, and Abraham naming the place Beersheba. Here Isaac, Abimelech and Phicol swear, a well is found, and Beersheba is named again. Traditional readers see a son renewing his father's treaty and his father's place-names (as in 26:18). Many critical scholars see two versions of one local tradition that explained the name. Literary readers point out the contrast: Abraham dealt from strength, while Isaac is sought out by the men who drove him away, because "the LORD has been with you."

a: Shibah
p: Shibah can mean "seven" or "oath." Beersheba is "Well of the Oath" or "Well of Seven."
b: In Hebrew "to swear" (nishba') is related to "seven" (sheva'), perhaps because oaths were sealed with seven of something (21:28–31). Shibah here sounds like both, and the oath of 26:31 has just been sworn. Beersheba (Be'er sheva') is "Well of the Oath" or "Well of Seven." The Septuagint translated Shibah as "Oath."

a: Beersheba
p: The excavated city at Tel Beersheba is from the Iron Age, centuries after any date for Isaac.
b: Excavations at Tel Beersheba (Yohanan Aharoni, 1969–76) found a planned Iron Age town with a large horned altar, but no settlement there from the Middle or Late Bronze Age, the usual dates proposed for the patriarchs. Critical scholars such as Finkelstein take this as a sign that the stories reflect the world of later Israel. Conservative scholars reply that Genesis never puts a city here in Isaac's day: the patriarchs camp at wells, and the "city" of 26:33 is the narrator's "to this day." Modern Beersheba lies a few miles to the west of the ancient mound.

a: At forty years of age
p: Isaac married at forty (25:20). The rabbis saw Esau copying his father's outward pattern.
b: Isaac was forty when he married Rebekah (25:20), and now Esau marries at forty too, but he marries two women of Canaan, the very thing Abraham forbade for Isaac (24:3). Genesis Rabbah compares Esau to the pig of Psalm 80:13, which lies down and stretches out its split hooves as if to say "I am clean": Esau spent forty years seizing other men's wives, the midrash says, and then claimed he was following his father's example. Hebrews 12:16 likewise calls him "sexually immoral or godless." Neither charge is in Genesis itself, which simply says the marriages grieved his parents.

a: Beeri the Hittite's
p: Not the empire in Turkey: "Hittites" in Genesis are a local people, "the sons of Heth" around Hebron.
b: The great Hittite empire ruled central Anatolia (modern Turkey) from about 1650 to 1180 BC, and its kings never governed the hills of Canaan. Genesis means something else: "Heth" is a son of Canaan (10:15), and "the sons of Heth" are a local group near Hebron who sold Abraham his burial cave (23:3–20). Scholars debate whether they were a remnant of northern peoples or simply had a similar name. Either way, for Isaac and Rebekah they are "women of this land" (27:46), outside the family.

a: his eyes had grown too dim to see
p: The midrash offers three reasons, one of them that God dimmed his eyes so Jacob could receive the blessing.
b: Rashi, drawing on Genesis Rabbah, gives three answers. First, the smoke of the incense Esau's wives offered to their idols damaged his eyes. Second, when Isaac lay bound on the altar (22:9), the angels wept and their tears fell into his eyes. Third, God dimmed his sight so that Jacob could take the blessing. Literary readers notice that the whole chapter runs on the senses: Isaac cannot see, so he hears, touches, tastes and smells, and every one of them is fooled except his hearing (27:22).

a: so that my soul may bless you
p: In the ancient world a father's last words could settle the inheritance, and they could not be taken back.
b: "My soul" (nafshi) means "I myself, with all my being." A blessing spoken by a father near death was more than a wish. Speiser pointed to a lawsuit from Nuzi, a Hurrian town of the 1400s BC, in which a court upheld what a dying father had said to his son. In Genesis such words shape the future (48:8–20; 49:1–28), and they cannot be withdrawn (27:33). This is why the meal matters: eating together and the words that follow form a solemn act, not a snack.

a: Rebekah was listening
p: She knew the oracle that "the elder will serve the younger" (25:23). Readers have judged her very differently.
b: Rebekah alone heard God say that the older twin would serve the younger (see 25:23). Many Jewish and Christian readers defend her: she acted to carry out God's word when Isaac was about to ignore it (on the Targum's "by prophecy," see 27:13). Calvin praised her faith but condemned her method. Others see a favoritism that matches Isaac's (25:28) and a deception that costs her dearly: she sends Jacob away "a few days" and never sees him again. The narrator does not comment, but the rest of Jacob's life shows deceit coming back on the deceiver.

a: a man playing a trick on him
p: Jacob objects to the plan, but only because it might fail. He never says it is wrong.
b: The word metatea' means someone who makes a fool of another, a mocker or trickster (2 Chronicles 36:16). Jacob's fear is practical: if he is caught, he will look like a cheat and earn a curse. He does not object that it would be a lie. Rebekah's reply in 27:13 answers exactly that fear and no other.

a: Let your curse fall on me
p: The official Aramaic translation adds that Rebekah had learned by prophecy that no curse would come.
b: Targum Onqelos, the Aramaic translation read in synagogues, renders this verse: "To me it was said in prophecy that the curses will not come on you, my son." The rabbis thus made Rebekah a prophet acting on God's word, not a schemer. Many modern readers prefer the plain sense: a mother willing to take any consequence for the son she loves. Ironically, the curse that falls on her is the loss of that son.

a: the best clothes of Esau
p: The midrash told many stories about these clothes: Adam's garments, Nimrod's, or the robes of the firstborn as priest.
b: The Hebrew calls them hachamudot, "the desirable ones." Jewish tradition wondered why Esau's best clothes were kept at his mother's house. One midrash says they were the garments God made for Adam (3:21), passed down through Nimrod; Rashi mentions the Nimrod story. Another holds that the firstborn served as the family priest before the Levites and wore special robes for sacrifice. Some Christian preachers have read Jacob in his brother's clothes as a picture of the believer clothed in Christ, the true firstborn (Galatians 3:27). The text itself simply sets up the next scene: Isaac will smell these clothes.

a: Because the LORD your God made it come my way
t: Using God's name in a lie
p: Jacob calls him "the LORD your God," not "my God." He will not say "my God" until his vow in 28:21.
b: This is the boldest line of the deception: Jacob brings God into the lie. Notice also his words: "the LORD your God." Jacob does not yet call the LORD his own God. The next time he speaks of God this way he is alone at Bethel, and his vow ends, "then the LORD will be my God" (28:21). Many readers see the whole Jacob story as the slow change from the first phrase to the second.

a: The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are Esau's hands
t: The voice of Jacob and the hands of Esau
p: The Talmud turned this line into a saying about Israel's prayer and Rome's power.
b: In Jewish tradition Esau stands for Edom, and Edom later for Rome. The Talmud (Gittin 57b) reads Isaac's words as a picture of history: "the voice" is the cry Rome's armies drew from Israel in the wars with Rome, and "the hands" are the hands that killed. Genesis Rabbah reverses it into hope: as long as the voice of Jacob is heard in houses of prayer and study, the hands of Esau have no power. The line has become a proverb for the choice between words and force.

a: and he blessed him
p: Isaac "blessed him" here, but the blessing itself comes four verses later. Why?
b: The narrative seems to reach its end twice: Isaac blesses Jacob after touching him (27:23), and again after kissing and smelling him (27:27). Gunkel and many critical scholars saw two older versions woven together: one in which touch decided the matter and one in which smell did. Others read 27:23 as a summary of what is about to happen, a common Hebrew way of telling, or take the first "blessed" as a greeting. Either way, the delay makes the reader wait through Isaac's last doubt in 27:24.

a: is like the smell of a field
t: The smell of a blessed field
p: The clothes of the outdoorsman smell of open country. Rashi says they carried the smell of the Garden of Eden.
b: Esau is the man of the field (25:27), and his clothes smell of it. To the blind father the scent becomes a picture of the land itself, fertile and blessed by God. Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah, says that the smell was not of goat but of the Garden of Eden, which came in with Jacob. Paul later uses scent as a picture of God's people: "the fragrance of Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:15).

a: some of the dew of the sky
t: Dew and the richness of the earth
p: In Canaan's rainless summers, dew kept crops alive. Moses' blessing uses the same words for all Israel.
b: Canaan depends on rain in winter and heavy night dew in the dry summer. "The dew of the sky" and "the richness of the earth" together mean a fertile, well-watered land. Moses' last blessing promises Israel the same: a land "of grain and new wine, where the skies drip with dew" (Deuteronomy 33:28). The words come back, turned around, in Esau's blessing (27:39).

a: Be master over your brothers
t: The older will serve the younger
p: The blessing confirms the oracle of 25:23. Paul uses this story in Romans 9.
b: "Be master over your brothers" puts into Isaac's mouth what God had told Rebekah: "the elder will serve the younger" (25:23). David later subdued Edom (2 Samuel 8:14). "Whoever curses you, cursed" repeats God's promise to Abraham (12:3), and Balaam will say it of Israel (Numbers 24:9). In Romans 9:10–13 Paul uses the twins to argue that God's choice "stands not by works but by him who calls," and quotes Malachi 1:2–3, "Jacob I loved. But Esau I hated." Augustine and Calvin read this as individual election to salvation. Many other interpreters, Jewish and Christian, hold that Genesis and Malachi speak of two peoples and their roles in history, not the eternal fate of two men.

a: Yes, and blessed he will be
t: Why can't Isaac take it back?
p: Isaac trembles, but he confirms the blessing. Hebrews says Esau found no way to change it, though he wept.
b: Many readers say that in that culture a spoken blessing, once given, could not be recalled, like an arrow already shot. Others note that Isaac does not try: his great trembling suggests he suddenly sees that God's choice (25:23) has overruled his own. Hebrews 11:20 counts this as faith: "By faith Isaac gave Jacob and Esau a blessing that reached even to things still to come." Hebrews 12:17 adds that Esau "found no place for repentance, though he searched for it with tears." Interpreters debate whose change of mind he could not find: Isaac's, or Esau's own heart.

a: a great and bitter cry
p: The same words describe Mordecai's cry in Esther 4:1. The midrash connected the two.
b: "A great and bitter cry" (tse'aqah gedolah umarah) appears only here and in Esther 4:1, where Mordecai cries out at Haman's plot. Genesis Rabbah draws a line between them: Jacob made Esau cry out once, and Jacob's descendants were repaid with a cry in Shushan, when Haman, a descendant of Esau's grandson Amalek (36:12; 1 Samuel 15:8; Esther 3:1), tried to destroy them. The midrash refuses to let Jacob's victory erase Esau's pain.

a: He has grabbed me by the heel
p: Jacob's name sounds like "heel" and like "cheat." Birthright and blessing are a pun too.
b: Jacob (Ya'aqov) was named for grabbing his brother's heel ('aqev) at birth (25:26). The verb 'aqav also means "to cheat, trip up." Jeremiah uses it for a treacherous brother: "every brother is a heel-grabber" ('aqov ya'qov, Jeremiah 9:4), and Hosea recalls the heel (Hosea 12:3). Esau adds a second pun: "my birthright" (bekhorati) and "my blessing" (birkhati) differ by one switched letter pair. Note that Esau now blames Jacob for the birthright he himself sold (25:33).

a: away from the richness of the earth
p: The KJV reads "thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth." Most now read "away from." The Hebrew allows both.
b: Isaac repeats the exact words of Jacob's blessing (27:28): "from the richness of the earth ... from the dew of the sky." The Hebrew preposition min can mean "some of" or "away from." In 27:28 it clearly means "some of." The KJV and some older readers took it the same way here, giving Esau a lesser share of the same gifts. Most modern scholars read "away from," since 27:37 says Isaac has nothing left to give, and Edom's land south of the Dead Sea is largely dry hills and desert. The echo is deliberate either way: same words, different future.

a: But when you break loose
t: Edom will throw off the yoke
p: An uncertain verb: "roam," "grow restless" or "break free." History records Edom's revolt.
b: The verb tarid is rare (Jeremiah 2:31; Psalm 55:2) and may mean "roam freely," "grow restless" or "break loose." The KJV's "when thou shalt have the dominion" follows another guess. The sense is clear: Edom will serve Israel and then shake it off. David conquered Edom (2 Samuel 8:13–14), and in the days of King Joram of Judah, around 845 BC, "Edom revolted out from under Judah's hand" (2 Kings 8:20–22). Critical scholars often date the blessing's final form after that revolt; traditional readers see a prophecy.

a: The days of mourning for my father are drawing near
p: Esau plans to wait until Isaac dies. Isaac in fact lives about twenty more years (35:28–29).
b: Esau will not kill his brother while their father is alive, perhaps out of respect, perhaps to avoid grieving him. Isaac, who thought he was near death in 27:2, lives on: he is still alive when Jacob returns twenty years later (35:27–29). The sons who were rivals at his blessing will stand together at his grave. The later prophets condemn Edom for exactly what Esau plans here: "violence to your brother Jacob" (Obadiah 10; Amos 1:11).

a: Why should I be robbed of you both in a single day?
p: If Esau killed Jacob, the family's own avenger might kill Esau. Rashi saw a hidden prophecy.
b: In ancient Israel a murderer's life was forfeit to the "avenger of blood" from the victim's family (Numbers 35:19). The widow of Tekoa uses the same fear to move David: one son killed the other, and now the family wants to kill the survivor (2 Samuel 14:6–7). So Rebekah fears losing both. Rashi, following the Talmud (Sotah 13a), sees an unknowing prophecy: Esau and Jacob were buried on the same day, after a scuffle at Jacob's funeral. Her real loss is quieter. Rebekah never appears again; we hear only of her nurse's death (35:8) and her grave (49:31).

a: I am sick of living because of the daughters of Heth
t: A second reason for Jacob to leave
p: Here Jacob leaves to find a wife. In 27:42–45 he leaves to escape Esau. One story or two?
b: Rebekah gives Isaac a different reason for sending Jacob away: not Esau's threat but marriage. Most critical scholars assign 26:34–35 and 27:46–28:9 to the Priestly source (P), which tells the patriarchs' story without the deceptions and makes Jacob's journey a proper search for a bride. Traditional readers see a wise woman: she tells her husband what he can accept and lets him send Jacob off with a full, knowing blessing (28:1–4). In either reading, the chapter that began with Isaac in control ends with Rebekah quietly steering him again.

a: So Isaac called Jacob and blessed him
p: This time there is no disguise. Isaac gives Jacob "the blessing of Abraham" with open eyes.
b: Whatever happened in chapter 27, Isaac now blesses Jacob on purpose and adds the heart of the covenant: "the blessing of Abraham" and the land (28:4). For traditional readers this settles the question of whether a stolen blessing counts: Isaac confirms it. Critical scholars assign 27:46–28:9 to the Priestly source, in which there was no trick at all, only a dutiful son sent to marry within the family. The final text keeps both pictures side by side.

a: Paddan-aram
p: "The plain of Aram," the region around Haran in what is now southeastern Turkey.
b: Paddan-aram is the Priestly writer's name for the area around Haran, on the Balikh River in upper Mesopotamia, about 450 miles northeast of Beersheba. Hosea calls it "the field of Aram" (Hosea 12:12). Paddan may come from an Aramaic word for "field" or an Akkadian word for "road." Haran was a major caravan city with a temple to the moon god Sin; Abraham's family had settled there (11:31; 24:10). The ruins at Harran still stand.

a: God Almighty
p: The patriarchs' special name for God (17:1; Exodus 6:3). Its meaning is debated.
b: El Shaddai is the name God gave himself to Abraham (17:1), and Exodus 6:3 says it was how he was known to the patriarchs before the name YHWH was explained. The traditional rendering "Almighty" comes from the Greek and Latin translations. Rabbinic tradition explained it as "the one who is sufficient" (she-dai). Many modern scholars link it to an Akkadian word for "mountain," "God of the mountain(s)," or to shad, "breast," since the name often comes with promises of fertility, as here and in 49:25. See 17:1.

a: an assembly of peoples
p: The word qahal later names Israel gathered before God. The Greek here says "a synagogue of nations."
b: Qahal, "assembly, congregation," becomes the word for Israel gathered at Sinai and in worship (Deuteronomy 9:10; 1 Kings 8:14). The Septuagint translates it here as synagōgē and elsewhere as ekklēsia, the word the New Testament uses for "church." The promise widens with each telling: "an assembly of peoples" here, "a nation and an assembly of nations" in 35:11.

a: Mahalath daughter of Ishmael
t: Esau tries to please his father
p: Esau marries into Abraham's family, but through Ishmael, the son who was also sent away.
b: Esau finally understands that his Canaanite wives grieve his parents (26:35) and marries a cousin, a daughter of Ishmael. It is a well-meant but clumsy move: he adds a wife instead of changing course, and he chooses the line that had also been set aside (21:10–14). In 36:3 Ishmael's daughter is called Basemath; on Esau's wives' names, see 36:2.

a: He came upon the place
p: "The place" appears three times in this verse. The rabbis heard a name of God and a prayer.
b: The Hebrew says Jacob "came upon the place" (hammaqom), and the word comes three times in one verse. In rabbinic Hebrew HaMakom, "the Place," is a name for God, who is the place of the world. The verb "came upon" (paga') can also mean "to pray, plead" (Jeremiah 7:16). So the Talmud (Berakhot 26b) teaches that Abraham began the morning prayer (19:27), Isaac the afternoon prayer (24:63), and Jacob the evening prayer, here at sunset. Rashi and the midrash also identify "the place" with Mount Moriah, the later Temple Mount (22:2, 4).

a: He took one of the stones of the place
p: "Stones" here, but "the stone" in 28:18. The Talmud told a story to explain it.
b: Literally Jacob took "from the stones of the place" and in the morning he takes "the stone" (28:18). The Talmud (Chullin 91b) tells that the stones argued, each wanting the righteous man to rest his head on it, and God made them one stone. Rashi repeats the story. The plain sense is simpler: he took one stone from those lying there. It was not a pillow so much as a guard or headrest, and it becomes the monument of the night.

a: a stairway
p: Sullam appears only here. It is probably a stairway or ramp, like those on Mesopotamian temple towers.
b: The KJV made "Jacob's ladder" famous, but sullam is found nowhere else in the Bible. It probably comes from salal, "to heap up," and many scholars link it to the Akkadian simmiltu, "stairway." Angels going up and down at the same time suggests a broad stairway or ramp rather than a narrow ladder. Mesopotamian temple towers (ziggurats) had great stairways up which worshipers climbed toward the god's shrine at the top.

a: its top reaching the sky
p: The builders of Babel wanted a tower "with its head in the heavens" (11:4). Here God sets up the stairway himself.
b: The phrase "its top reaching the sky" (rosho maggia' hashamaymah) echoes Babel, whose builders wanted "a tower with its head in the heavens" (11:4), the same Hebrew words. Babylon's own name was understood as Bab-ili, "Gate of God," and Jacob calls this place "heaven's gate" (28:17). Many scholars think a ziggurat lies behind the picture, and the link is likely. The difference is the point: at Babel people climb up to make a name for themselves; at Bethel nobody climbs, and God comes down to a man asleep on the ground with nothing in his hands.

a: going up and going down on it
p: Jesus says Nathanael will see "God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man" (John 1:51).
b: Notice the order: going up first. The angels are already on earth with Jacob. The Hebrew bo, "on it," can also mean "on him." Genesis Rabbah records a debate between Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yannai: were the angels going up and down on the stairway, or on Jacob? The second view said they went up to see Jacob's face engraved on God's throne and came down to see him sleeping. Jesus takes up the same picture in John 1:51: "you will see heaven standing open, and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man." He presents himself as the stairway, the meeting place of heaven and earth, and Nathanael as a true Israelite in whom there is no deceit, unlike the young Jacob (John 1:47).

a: the LORD stood above it
t: Above the stairway or beside Jacob?
p: The Hebrew 'alav can mean "above it" or "over him, beside him."
b: Nitsav 'alav may mean the LORD stood at the top of the stairway, or stood over Jacob, beside him on the ground, as the three men "stood over" Abraham in 18:2. Both are possible, and translators divide. The first fits the vision; the second fits the promise that follows: "I am with you" (28:15). This is the first time God speaks to Jacob, and he introduces himself as the God of Jacob's fathers.

a: you will break out westward and eastward
p: Parats means to break through. It becomes the word for Jacob's wealth in 30:30 and 30:43.
b: The verb parats means "to burst out, break through," like a flood or a breach in a wall. The promise to Jacob is not slow growth but an explosion in every direction. The same verb describes how Jacob's flocks "burst out" in 30:30 and 30:43, and it gives Perez his name (38:29), Judah's son and David's ancestor. On the blessing for "all the clans of the earth," see 26:4.

a: I will not let go of you
p: This promise to a runaway becomes one of the Bible's central promises, down to "I myself am with you every day."
b: "I am with you ... I will not let go of you" is spoken to a man running for his life with nothing. The promise is repeated to Jacob on his return (31:3), to Joshua (Joshua 1:5), to the exiles (Isaiah 41:10), and finally by Jesus: "I myself am with you every day, until the completion of the age" (Matthew 28:20). Hebrews 13:5 quotes the related promise "I will never leave you nor abandon you." Note the conditions: there are none. God does not ask Jacob to change first.

a: and I did not know it
p: Rashi: had I known, I would not have slept in such a holy place.
b: Rashi reads Jacob's words as regret: if he had known, he would not have lain down to sleep there. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, take the line more widely: God is present in places that look ordinary and in lives that do not seem ready for him. The surprise is real in the text: Jacob had not sought God, and the place was not yet a shrine.

a: heaven's gate
t: House of God and gate of heaven
p: Churches have long used this verse at their dedication. For Babylon, "gate of God," see 28:12.
b: Jacob names the place twice: "house of God" (beit Elohim, the origin of Bethel) and "gate of heaven." The words were later applied to the Temple, where heaven and earth met. In the Latin liturgy, the opening chant for the dedication of a church is Terribilis est locus iste, "How fearsome is this place: it is the house of God and the gate of heaven." Christian readers also link the verse to Jesus, who calls his body the temple (John 2:19–21) and himself "the door" (John 10:9).
orig: בֵּית אֱלֹהִים ... שַׁעַר הַשָּׁמָיִם (beit Elohim ... sha'ar hashamayim)

a: set it up as a standing stone
p: Standing stones marked holy places all over Canaan. Later law banned them.
b: A matsevah is an upright stone set up as a memorial or a sign of a god's presence. Archaeologists have found them across the region: the row of ten great stones at Middle Bronze Age Gezer, a stone in the inner shrine of the Iron Age temple at Arad, and many smaller ones. Jacob sets up several (31:45; 35:14, 20). Later the law forbids them as Canaanite (Deuteronomy 16:22; Leviticus 26:1), though Hosea can still list them as normal (Hosea 3:4). Critical scholars see this story as the founding legend of the Bethel shrine, which became a royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29). Pouring oil marked the stone as set apart for God.

a: Bethel
p: "House of God." Usually identified with Beitin, about 12 miles north of Jerusalem.
b: Since Edward Robinson's survey in 1838, most scholars have identified Bethel with the village of Beitin, north of Jerusalem; a minority prefer nearby el-Bireh. Luz, "almond tree," was the Canaanite town's name (Judges 1:23–26). Abraham had already camped and built an altar near Bethel (12:8; 13:3). After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam set up a golden calf there (1 Kings 12:29), Amos called it "the king's sanctuary" (Amos 7:13), and Hosea mocked it as Beth-aven, "house of wickedness" (Hosea 4:15). Josiah finally tore down its altar (2 Kings 23:15).

a: Then Jacob made a vow
p: "If God will be with me ..." Is Jacob setting terms for God? It depends partly on where the "then" begins.
b: Many readers hear Jacob bargaining: he repeats what God has just promised and makes his loyalty depend on it. Others note that a vow in Israel always had this shape, "if you do this, I will do that" (Numbers 21:2; Judges 11:30; 1 Samuel 1:11), and that Jacob only asks for what God already offered. The grammar is also debated. Most translations make the "then" begin with "the LORD will be my God" (28:21). Rashi takes that line as part of the request (that God's name rest on him and his children) and begins the vow itself in 28:22: the stone will be God's house, and he will give a tenth.

a: a tenth, a tenth to you
t: The first promise of a tithe
p: "Tithing I will tithe it." Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek (14:20); Jacob promises one to God.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb: 'asser a'asrennu, "I will surely tithe it." Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils to Melchizedek (14:20); Jacob's is the first promise of a regular tithe. Israel's law later made the tithe a duty (Leviticus 27:30–32; Deuteronomy 14:22–29), and Amos mocks the people who brought tithes to Bethel while oppressing the poor (Amos 4:4). Genesis never says when or how Jacob kept the vow, though God reminds him of it (31:13; 35:1).

a: the land of the people of the east
p: Bene qedem: the peoples east and northeast of Canaan, from the Syrian desert to Mesopotamia.
b: "The people of the east" (bene qedem) is a loose name for the herders and townspeople beyond the Jordan and the Euphrates: Job was "Of all the people of the East, he was the greatest" (Job 1:3), and they raid Israel with the Midianites in Judges 6:3. The journey from Beersheba to Haran is roughly 450 to 500 miles, many weeks on foot. Genesis skips the whole trip in one verse and slows down again at a well.

a: there was a well in the open field
p: Rebekah, Rachel and Zipporah were each first met at a well. John 4 sets Jesus at Jacob's well.
b: Robert Alter called this a "type-scene," a standard scene that Israel's storytellers retold with telling changes. A man travels to a foreign land, meets a young woman at a well, someone draws water, she runs home, and a marriage follows: Abraham's servant and Rebekah (24:10–27), Jacob and Rachel here, Moses and Zipporah (Exodus 2:15–21). The changes reveal character. Abraham's servant prays; Jacob shows off his strength. John 4 plays on the pattern: at "Jacob's well" Jesus, who calls himself the bridegroom (John 3:29), asks a Samaritan woman for water and offers her living water.

a: Laban, Nahor's son
p: Laban is the son of Bethuel and grandson of Nahor (24:15, 29). Hebrew "son" covers any descendant.
b: Laban's father was Bethuel, and Bethuel's father was Nahor, Abraham's brother (22:20–23; 24:15, 29). Hebrew ben, "son," is used for any male descendant, so "son of Nahor" means "of Nahor's family." The same usage lets Matthew call Jesus "son of David, son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Nahor is the family's well-known ancestor, and the shepherds know the name.

a: rolled the stone off the mouth of the well
p: The shepherds needed everyone to move the stone. Jacob does it alone the moment he sees Rachel.
b: The shepherds have just said they cannot water the flocks until everyone gathers to move the stone (29:8). Jacob moves it by himself. Rashi comments that he did it "like someone pulling a stopper out of a bottle," to show his great strength. The narrator says "Laban his mother's brother" three times in one verse: Jacob is thinking of family, and of his mother. Readers often notice that the smooth man who stayed among the tents (25:27) turns out to be strong.

a: he raised his voice and wept
p: Rashi gives two reasons: he came empty-handed, and he foresaw that Rachel would not be buried with him.
b: Rashi offers two midrashic reasons. First, Abraham's servant had come with ten camels of gifts (24:10), but Jacob came with nothing: in the midrash, Esau's son Eliphaz chased him and took all he had. Second, Jacob saw by the holy spirit that Rachel would not be buried beside him (35:19; 49:31). The plain sense is enough: a fugitive, alone for weeks, suddenly finds his family.

a: You really are my bone and my flesh
p: The language of kinship, first spoken by Adam over Eve (2:23).
b: "My bone and my flesh" means "my own close kin." Adam says it of Eve (2:23), Abimelech of his mother's clan (Judges 9:2), and the tribes of David (2 Samuel 5:1). Coming from Laban, it is warm but double-edged: he will treat Jacob as family when it profits him and as a hired hand when it does not (29:15).

a: Leah's eyes were soft
p: "Weak," "tender" or "delicate"? The Hebrew rakkot is unclear, and the rabbis said she had wept.
b: Rakkot means "soft, tender" (18:7; 33:13). It may mean dull or weak, in contrast to Rachel's beauty, or it may be a compliment: lovely, gentle eyes, but Rachel was beautiful all over. The Talmud (Bava Batra 123a) and Rashi say Leah's eyes were weak from weeping, because people said the older daughter would marry the older son, Esau, and she prayed to be spared. The names may also matter: Rachel means "ewe" (Isaiah 53:7), and Leah may mean "cow" (from an Akkadian word), both fitting a herding family.

a: I will work for you seven years
t: Work instead of a bride price
p: A groom usually paid the bride's father. Jacob has nothing, so he offers seven years of work.
b: Israel's law and other ancient laws expected a groom to pay a bride price (mohar) to the bride's family (34:12; Exodus 22:16–17; 1 Samuel 18:25). Jacob arrived with nothing, so he pays in labor. Seven years is far more than any known price, a measure of how much he loves Rachel. Laban's daughters later complain that he kept everything for himself (31:15).

a: they were like a few days
p: Rebekah sent Jacob away for "a few days" (27:44). The same words now mean seven years of love.
b: The Hebrew yamim achadim, "a few days," is exactly what Rebekah promised in 27:44: stay with Laban "a few days" until Esau calms down. Those few days have become seven years, and will become twenty (31:41), but to a man in love they pass like a few days. It is one of the most tender lines in Genesis.

a: he took Leah his daughter and brought her to Jacob
p: A veiled bride, a dark tent, a night of drinking. The Talmud adds that Rachel helped her sister.
b: Brides were veiled (24:65), the wedding feast was a drinking feast (mishteh), and the tent was dark. Still, readers have asked how Jacob was fooled. The Talmud (Megillah 13b; Bava Batra 123a) says that Jacob had agreed on secret signs with Rachel, and that Rachel, seeing her sister about to be shamed, gave them to Leah. Jewish tradition holds up this act as Rachel's great kindness; Lamentations Rabbah (proem 24) makes it the reason God listens when Rachel weeps for her children (Jeremiah 31:15).

a: In the morning, there she was: Leah!
p: Jacob disguised himself as the older brother. Now the older sister is disguised as the younger.
b: The pattern is exact. Jacob, the younger, took the place of the firstborn in the dark of his father's blindness; now Leah, the older, takes the place of the younger in the dark of the wedding tent. Laban's reply turns the knife: "It is not done this way in our place, giving the younger before the firstborn" (29:26). The word bekhirah, "firstborn," recalls Jacob's "It is I, Esau, your firstborn" (27:19). J. P. Fokkelman traces this measure-for-measure pattern through the whole Jacob cycle. Genesis Rabbah (70:19) imagines Leah's answer in the morning: "Didn't your father call you Esau, and you answered him?"

a: Why have you tricked me?
p: Rimmah is the same root as the "trickery" with which Jacob took the blessing (27:35).
b: The verb rimmitani, "you tricked me," comes from the root of mirmah, "deceit, trickery," the word Isaac used of Jacob (27:35). Jacob's sons will answer Shechem "with trickery" (bemirmah, 34:13). The Plain English Translation uses "trickery" in all three places so the reader can hear the one word. The narrator never says "Jacob was punished," but the one word tells the reader all that is needed.

a: Finish this one's wedding week
p: Weddings lasted seven days. Jacob gets Rachel after one week and pays for her with seven more years.
b: Wedding feasts lasted seven days (Judges 14:12, 17; compare Tobit 11:18). Laban does not make Jacob wait another seven years to marry Rachel: he marries her a week later and then works seven years to pay. So Jacob has two wives, sisters, within eight days, and each sister comes with her own slave woman (29:24, 29), who will also bear his children.

a: Laban gave him Rachel his daughter as his wife
p: The law of Moses forbids marrying two sisters (Leviticus 18:18). How could Jacob do it?
b: Leviticus 18:18 forbids taking a woman's sister as a rival wife while she lives. Jacob's household shows why: jealousy, competition and grief (30:1, 15). Jewish interpreters who held that the patriarchs kept the Torah (26:5) had to explain this. Ramban answered that they kept it only in the land of Israel, and Jacob married in Haran; he adds that Rachel died just as Jacob entered the land for good (35:16–19). Most readers simply see a story told from before the law, and the law as later wisdom drawn from stories like this one.

a: the unloved one
p: The Hebrew says Leah was "hated." 29:30 shows what it means: loved less than Rachel.
b: Literally, "the LORD saw that Leah was hated" (senu'ah). The verse before has just said Jacob "loved Rachel more than Leah." In Hebrew, "love" and "hate" side by side often mean "prefer" and "prefer less." The law of Deuteronomy 21:15–17 describes exactly Jacob's case, a man with a loved and a "hated" wife, and rules that the firstborn of the less-loved wife keeps his right. The same idiom stands behind Malachi 1:2–3 and Romans 9:13, "I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau," and behind Jesus' "hate father and mother" (Luke 14:26; compare Matthew 10:37, "love more").

a: called his name Reuben
t: Names as cries of the heart
p: Each name is a pun on what Leah feels, not a dictionary meaning.
b: Reuben sounds like re'u ben, "look, a son!", and Leah explains it as ra'ah be'onyi, "he has looked on my misery," with a further echo in ye'ehavani, "he will love me." Simeon (Shim'on) comes from shama', "he heard." Levi sounds like yillaveh, "he will be joined." Judah (Yehudah) sounds like odeh, "I will praise." Hebrew naming stories work by sound, not by historical root. Leah's first three names hope for Jacob's love; her fourth turns from Jacob to God.

a: my husband will join himself to me
p: The tribe of Levi is later "joined" to Aaron to serve at the tabernacle, the same pun.
b: Leah hopes Jacob will finally be "joined" (yillaveh) to her. Numbers 18:2 and 18:4 play on the same pun for Levi's descendants: they "join" Aaron and serve the sanctuary. Leah's son, born of a hope for human love, becomes the father of Israel's priestly tribe. Note also that the Hebrew says "he called his name," probably meaning "his name was called"; whether Jacob or Leah named him is unclear.

a: This time I will praise the LORD
p: The Talmud says no one had praised God until Leah did. From Judah come David, the Jews, and, for Christians, Jesus.
b: The Talmud (Berakhot 7b) quotes Rabbi Yochanan: "From the day the Holy One created the world, no one praised him until Leah came and praised him." Her earlier names asked for something; this one gives thanks. From Judah come the royal line of David (49:10; Ruth 4:18–22) and the name "Jew" (Yehudi). For Christians, Jesus is "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5; Hebrews 7:14). The unloved wife becomes the mother of Israel's kings and of its priests.

a: Give me children!
p: The midrash rebukes Jacob: is that how you answer a woman in distress?
b: Rachel's cry, "Give me children, or I am a dead woman," turns out to be bitterly true: she dies giving birth to her second son (35:16–19). Jacob's answer is theologically right (only God opens the womb) and humanly cold. Genesis Rabbah imagines God answering Jacob: "Is that how one answers a woman in distress? By your life, your sons will one day stand before her son," meaning Joseph, before whom the brothers bow in Egypt. Hannah's prayer is the contrast: she takes the same grief to God (1 Samuel 1:10–11).

a: so that she can give birth on my knees
t: A slave woman as surrogate mother
p: Ancient marriage contracts let a childless wife give her slave to her husband. The child counted as hers.
b: Sarah did the same with Hagar (16:1–4). The Laws of Hammurabi (sections 144–147) and an Old Assyrian marriage contract describe childless wives providing a slave woman for their husbands; a contract from Nuzi requires a wife who bears no children to give her husband a slave woman. Giving birth "on my knees" probably describes a rite of adoption: the newborn was placed on the knees of its legal mother (compare 48:12; 50:23; Job 3:12). For the enslaved women, Bilhah and Zilpah, there was no choice, and the text gives them no words.

a: I too can be built up through her
p: "Be built" (ibbaneh) sounds like ben, "son." Sarah used the same words for Hagar (16:2).
b: The verb banah, "to build," sounds like ben, "son," and banim, "children." A family is a "house" that is built by children (Ruth 4:11, of Rachel and Leah). Rachel repeats Sarah's words to Abraham exactly (16:2). The pun cannot be carried into English; the gloss gives the sense.

a: God has judged for me
p: Dan means "he judged"; Naphtali sounds like "my wrestling." Rachel sees her rivalry as a struggle before God.
b: Danani Elohim, "God has judged for me," that is, given me justice, gives Dan his name. Naphtali comes from naftulei Elohim niftalti (30:8), "wrestlings of God I have wrestled." Rachel uses the courtroom and the wrestling match, and both pictures point forward to Jacob, who will wrestle with God himself at the Jabbok (32:24–28).

a: I have wrestled God's wrestlings
p: Elohim can mean "God" or work as a superlative, "mighty." Both readings are possible here.
b: Hebrew sometimes uses Elohim, "God," to mean "very great": "a prince of God" (23:6) means a mighty prince, and Nineveh is "a city great in God's eyes" (Jonah 3:3; the Hebrew says literally "great to God"). So naftulei Elohim may mean "mighty wrestlings," as many translations have it. It may also mean a contest over God's favor, or wrestlings with God himself in prayer. The Plain English Translation keeps "God's wrestlings" so the reader can hear the link with Jacob's night at the Jabbok (32:28: "you have struggled with God ... and have won").

a: Good fortune has come!
p: Gad means "good fortune." The KJV's "a troop cometh" took the name from another word.
b: Gad means "luck, good fortune," and Gad was also the name of a god of fortune worshiped in the region (Isaiah 65:11, "who lay out a table for Luck"). The KJV's "A troop cometh" followed older Jewish interpreters who linked the name to gedud, "raiding band," which is the pun Jacob uses in 49:19 ("Gad, raiders will raid him"). On the written and read forms of the Hebrew, see the textual note.

a: For daughters will call me happy
p: Leah's words are echoed by Mary in Luke 1:48. Asher means "happy."
b: Asher is from ishsheruni, "they will call me happy." In the Septuagint, Leah says "the women will call me blessed" (makariousin). Mary's song in Luke 1:48 uses the same Greek verb: "from now on all generations will call me blessed." Mary's song is full of Old Testament echoes, especially of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and this may be one of them. Leah's joy is for a son born through her slave; Mary's is for her own son.
orig: בְּאָשְׁרִי כִּי אִשְּׁרוּנִי בָּנוֹת (be'oshri ki ishsheruni banot)

a: came upon mandrakes
p: A plant famous for fertility and love magic. Rachel gets the mandrakes, but Leah gets the baby.
b: The mandrake (Mandragora officinarum) has a forked root that can look like a human body and yellow-orange fruit that ripens in May, at the wheat harvest. Its fruit has a strong scent (Song of Songs 7:13), and across the ancient world it was used as a love charm and fertility drug. The Hebrew duda'im sounds like dodim, "lovemaking." The story's irony is plain: Rachel trades for the magic, but Leah, who gave it up, conceives (30:17), and Rachel conceives only when "God remembered Rachel" (30:22).

a: I have hired you outright
p: Leah "hired" Jacob, and God "paid her wages." Issachar's name puns on both.
b: Leah says sakhor sekhartikha, "I have surely hired you," a bold, even comic line from the unloved wife. In 30:18 she says God gave her her sakhar, "wages," for giving her slave to Jacob. Issachar's name (Yissakhar) sounds like yesh sakhar, "there is a reward." The word "wages" runs through these chapters: Laban asks Jacob to name his wages (29:15; 30:28), and changes them ten times (31:7).

a: Now my husband will honor me
p: The verb zabal appears only here. It may mean "honor," "exalt" or "live with."
b: Leah makes two puns: zevadani ... zeved tov, "he has given me a good gift," and yizbeleni, which gives Zebulun his name. That verb is found nowhere else. Older translations guessed "dwell with me" (KJV), linking it to zevul, "lofty house" (1 Kings 8:13). Many scholars now compare a word in Ugaritic texts meaning "prince, exalted," found in the title zbl b'l, "Prince Baal," behind the New Testament's Beelzebul. So "honor" or "exalt" is likely. Leah, six sons later, still hopes for her husband's respect.

a: Dinah
p: Every son's name is explained; Dinah's is not. The Talmud tells why Leah prayed for a girl.
b: Every son's name gets an explanation; Dinah's does not. Her name means "judgment" or "vindication," the feminine form of Dan (30:6). Jacob may have had other daughters (37:35; 46:7), though Rashi reads "daughters" there as daughters-in-law. Only Dinah is named, because of what happens in chapter 34. The Talmud (Berakhot 60a) says Leah, knowing Jacob would have twelve sons, prayed that her seventh child would be a girl, so that Rachel would have at least as many sons as each of the slave women.

a: May the LORD add another son for me
p: Two puns at once: God has "taken away" (asaf) her shame; may he "add" (yosef) another son.
b: Rachel's first son gets a double explanation: asaf, "God has taken away my disgrace" (30:23), and yosef, "may the LORD add." Joseph's name is a prayer, and it is answered with Benjamin, at the cost of her life (35:16–19). After years of the name "God" in these birth stories, Rachel uses the personal name "the LORD" here, as Leah did in 29:32–35.
orig: יוֹסֵף (Yosef): אָסַף (asaf), "took away"; יֹסֵף (yosef), "may he add"

a: I have read the signs
p: Nichashti usually means "I have learned by divination." Some scholars read "I have grown rich."
b: The verb nichesh means to practice divination, reading omens (44:5, 15; 2 Kings 17:17), which the law later forbids (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10). Laban, a man with household gods (31:19), finds out by his own methods what the narrator already knows. Some scholars instead compare an Akkadian verb meaning "to prosper" and translate "I have grown rich, and the LORD has blessed me because of you." Either way, Laban admits the truth of 12:3: those who bless Abraham's family are blessed.

a: has burst out into a great deal
p: The same verb God used in 28:14: "you will break out." The promise works even in Laban's flock.
b: Parats, "burst out," is the verb of God's promise at Bethel (28:14), and it comes again in 30:43: "the man burst out very, very much." Jacob does not mention Bethel to Laban, but the reader hears it. On Jacob's "wherever I set my foot," see the gloss.

a: every speckled and spotted sheep
p: Near Eastern sheep were mostly white and goats mostly dark. Jacob asks only for the rare oddly colored ones.
b: In the region the usual sheep were white and the usual goats black or dark brown. Jacob asks for the exceptions: dark sheep and spotted or speckled goats. It looks like a modest bargain, and Laban agrees at once (30:34). Then he cheats even on that, removing all the off-colored animals before Jacob can start (30:35). Shepherds in that world often worked for a share of the newborn animals, and contracts like this are known from Mesopotamia.

a: poplar
p: Livneh ("white poplar") and "white" (lavan) both sound like Laban, "White."
b: Laban's name means "white." Jacob takes branches of livneh, a tree whose name also means "white" (white poplar or storax), and peels lavan, "white," stripes in them, "laying bare the white." The storyteller is having fun: Jacob beats "White" with white. Earlier, Jacob's brother was linked to "red" (adom, Edom, 25:30).

a: the flocks mated in front of the branches
p: Ancient people believed what a mother saw at conception marked her young. The text later credits God (31:9–12).
b: Many ancient and medieval people believed in "maternal impression," the idea that what a mother sees at conception shapes her offspring. Modern genetics rules out that the stripes on the branches caused the stripes on the lambs. Readers answer in different ways. Many traditional commentators, Jewish and Christian, say the method was Jacob's but the result was God's, as Jacob himself says in 31:9–12. Others note that Jacob also bred only the strong animals (30:41–42), and suggest he was practicing real selective breeding. Critical scholars often see two versions: one that credits Jacob's cleverness (30:37–43) and one that credits God's dream (31:10–12).

a: The man grew very, very rich
p: The fugitive who crossed the Jordan with only a staff (32:10) now has two camps.
b: The Hebrew says "the man burst out very, very" (30:43, literally; compare 30:30). The list of his wealth, flocks, slaves, camels and donkeys, matches Abraham's in 12:16 and Isaac's in 26:13–14. Jacob arrived with nothing but a staff (32:10). The next chapter shows what wealth brings: envy from Laban's sons (31:1), as it did from the Philistines (26:14).

a: all this wealth
p: Kavod means "heaviness," then "wealth" and "honor," and later "glory."
b: Kavod comes from the root "to be heavy." A heavy man is a rich and important one (13:2, "Abram was very heavy in livestock"). The same word later means God's "glory" (Exodus 33:18). Laban's sons use it with resentment: Jacob's importance has been built from their father's goods. Psalm 49:16–17 says that a man's kavod does not go down to the grave with him.

a: Return to the land of your fathers
p: "I will guard you everywhere you go and bring you back to this soil" (28:15). Now God says: go back.
b: At Bethel God promised, "I will guard you everywhere you go and bring you back to this soil" (28:15). Twenty years later the word comes: return. Jacob will retell it to his wives with more detail (31:11–13), naming "the God of Bethel." The promise "I will be with you" frames the whole journey, out and back.

a: changed my wages ten times
p: An idiom for "again and again," as in Numbers 14:22 and Job 19:3.
b: "Ten times" ('aseret monim) means "over and over," not an exact count: the Israelites tested God "ten times" (Numbers 14:22), and Job's friends insulted him "ten times" (Job 19:3). Jacob says it again in 31:41. Chapter 30 told only one bargain; this verse tells us Laban kept moving the goalposts, and 31:8 shows how God kept moving the lambs to match.

a: saw in a dream
p: Chapter 30 credits Jacob's branches. Here Jacob credits God's angel and a dream.
b: Jacob tells his wives that the striped flocks were God's doing: an angel showed him in a dream that only the spotted males were mating. There is no mention of peeled branches. Traditional readers see no conflict: Jacob used his skill, and God revealed that the outcome was his. Some add that the dream came first and the branches were Jacob's way of acting on it. Critical scholars often assign 30:37–43 and 31:4–16 to different sources (J and E). Literary readers note that Jacob tells the story in the way that best persuades his wives to leave.

a: The angel of God
t: The angel who speaks as God
p: The angel says "I am the God of Bethel" (31:13). Who is speaking?
b: In Genesis "the angel of God" or "the angel of the LORD" often speaks as God himself (16:10–13; 21:17–18; 22:11–18). Here the angel says, "I am the God of Bethel." Jewish interpreters usually take the angel as God's messenger speaking in his name, as an ambassador speaks for a king. Many early Christian writers saw the Son of God appearing before he became man. Critical scholars often see an older story of God appearing directly, later softened by adding "the angel." Jacob will meet this figure again at the Jabbok and in his blessing of Joseph's sons: "the angel who has redeemed me from all harm" (48:16).

a: He sold us
p: Normally part of the bride price came back to the bride. Laban kept all fourteen years of Jacob's work.
b: Rachel and Leah, rivals until now, speak with one voice against their father. In ancient Near Eastern practice, part of the bride price often went to the bride as her own security, as a dowry. Laban treated his daughters as goods for sale and "ate up" the price, Jacob's fourteen years of labor. Their words also mean they feel free to leave: their father has already cut them off.

a: the household gods
p: Small or large images of gods or ancestors, used in homes and for divination.
b: The teraphim were household images, perhaps of family gods or ancestors. They could be small enough to sit on (31:34) or the size of a man (1 Samuel 19:13, 16), and they were used for divination (Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2). Why did Rachel take them? In 1957 Anne Draffkorn argued from tablets at Nuzi that owning the household gods gave a claim to inheritance, and this view became popular. Moshe Greenberg (1962) and others showed the evidence is weak. Other suggestions: she wanted to wean her father from idols (Rashi), to stop him from learning by divination where they had gone (Ibn Ezra), to have their protection on the road, or simply to hurt him.

a: Jacob stole the heart of Laban the Aramean
p: Rachel stole the gods; Jacob "stole Laban's heart," a Hebrew idiom for deceiving him.
b: "To steal someone's heart" (ganav lev) means to fool him, leave him in the dark. The same verb, "steal," has just been used of Rachel (31:19), so the couple commits two thefts in two verses, each without the other knowing. Laban repeats the phrase in 31:26–27. Absalom later "stole the hearts" of Israel by flattery (2 Samuel 15:6). Jacob the trickster is still at work.
orig: וַיִּגְנֹב יַעֲקֹב אֶת־לֵב לָבָן (vayyignov Ya'aqov et-lev Lavan)

a: headed for the hill country of Gilead
t: A long way in ten days
p: From Haran to Gilead is about 350 miles. Can a household with flocks cover it in ten days?
b: Jacob had a three-day start (31:22), and Laban took seven days to catch him (31:23). Gilead, east of the Jordan, lies roughly 350 miles from Haran, a hard distance for flocks with young (33:13). Some scholars see a sign that the story has been compressed or that different traditions placed Laban's home in different regions. Others suggest Jacob's camp was a long way south of Haran when he left, or that the "seven days" is a round figure. The text does not say.

a: whether good or bad
p: An idiom: say nothing at all that would change the situation, neither threat nor bribe.
b: Literally, "lest you speak with Jacob from good to bad." Laban does speak to Jacob, at length, so the phrase does not forbid all speech. It probably means: do not try to change what has happened, whether by sweet talk or by force (compare 24:50; 2 Samuel 13:22). Laban repeats the warning himself in 31:29, a sign that it worked.

a: Whoever you find with your gods will not live
t: A curse on the one he loved
p: Jacob does not know Rachel has the gods. Rashi says his words led to her death.
b: Jacob swears an oath that puts the thief under a death sentence, not knowing he is speaking of Rachel. Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, says that because of this curse Rachel died on the road (35:16–19). Readers who do not take curses this way still feel the shadow: the next time Rachel is in danger, she dies.

a: the camel's saddle
p: Camels were in limited use early, but became common in Canaan only around 1000 BC.
b: The kar was probably a cushioned saddle with baskets. Camels appear often in the patriarch stories (24:10; 30:43; 31:17). Studies of animal bones, such as those from the copper mines of the Arava valley (Sapir-Hen and Ben-Yosef, 2013), suggest that domesticated camels became common in the southern Levant only around 1000 to 900 BC. Many critical scholars therefore see the camels as details from the writer's own time. Others, such as Kitchen, point to evidence that camels were domesticated in Arabia much earlier and used in small numbers, so a wealthy herdsman might well have them.

a: Laban felt through the whole tent
p: The verb is the one used when blind Isaac felt Jacob (27:12, 21–22). The deceiver's wife deceives her father.
b: Mishesh, "to feel, grope," appears in Genesis only in these two stories: Isaac feeling Jacob's goatskin hands (27:12, 21–22) and Laban feeling through Rachel's tent, and Jacob uses it again in 31:37. In both, a father gropes for the truth and is fooled by his own child. Jacob, who once fooled his father by touch, now benefits without knowing from the same trick.

a: The way of women is upon me
p: Rachel says she is having her period. The gods are hidden under a woman the law will call unclean.
b: "The way of women" means menstruation (compare 18:11). Rachel claims the custom that a woman in her period need not rise for her father, and Laban stops searching. Later law treats anything such a woman sits on as unclean (Leviticus 15:19–23). Whether or not she was telling the truth, the scene mocks the idols: Laban's gods cannot even protect themselves, and they spend the search under a woman's saddle. Isaiah mocks idols in the same spirit (Isaiah 46:1–2).

a: I took the loss myself
p: Ancient law let a shepherd clear himself for animals killed by wild beasts. Jacob paid anyway.
b: The Laws of Hammurabi (section 266) say that if a lion kills an animal in the fold, the shepherd clears himself by an oath before the god and the owner bears the loss. Exodus 22:10–13 says the same: if an animal is torn by a wild beast, the shepherd brings the remains as evidence and owes nothing. Amos 3:12 pictures a shepherd rescuing "two legs or a piece of an ear" as proof. Jacob claims he went beyond what any law required: he paid for the torn animals himself and even for those stolen.

a: the Fear of Isaac
p: A unique name for God: the One Isaac feared, or, as some propose, "the Kinsman of Isaac."
b: Pachad Yitschaq appears only here and in 31:53. Most interpreters understand "the One whom Isaac fears and worships." Some recall the terror of the near-sacrifice (22:9–12) or Isaac's trembling (27:33). W. F. Albright suggested "the Kinsman of Isaac," from a related Aramaic and Arabic word, and the idea was widely repeated; Delbert Hillers (1972) argued it lacks support. Albrecht Alt grouped the name with others like "the Mighty One of Jacob" (49:24) as names of a personal clan god. Jacob calls on God as his father's God: he has not yet said "my God."

a: let us cut a covenant
p: Hebrew "cuts" a covenant, probably from the animals cut in two to seal it (15:9–18).
b: The usual Hebrew phrase is karat berit, "to cut a covenant," probably from the rite in which animals were cut in half and the parties passed between them (15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18). This one is a treaty between equals, sealed by a stone, a heap, an oath and a shared meal (31:45–54). It marks a border more than a friendship: neither side may cross it to do harm (31:52).

a: Laban named it Jegar-sahadutha; Jacob named it Galeed
t: The first Aramaic in the Bible
p: Laban names the heap in Aramaic, Jacob in Hebrew. Both mean "heap of witness."
b: Yegar sahaduta is Aramaic, the language of Laban's people; Gal'ed is the same phrase in Hebrew. These two words are the first Aramaic in the Bible, and the two languages mark the border between the two peoples. Gal'ed also sounds like Gilead, the name of the hill country, so the verse explains that name too. Later, Aramaic became the common language of the Near East, used in parts of Ezra and Daniel and spoken by Jesus.

a: May the LORD keep watch between me and you
p: This verse is often used as a sweet blessing between parted friends. In context it is a threat.
b: Mizpah means "watchtower." Since the 1800s the line has been engraved on pairs of "Mizpah" coins and lockets and used as a farewell between friends and lovers. In the story, two men who do not trust each other call on God to watch the other one, so that neither can cheat when out of sight. It is a curse on the cheater, not a hug. The meaning that has grown around it is lovely, but it is not what Laban meant. The Septuagint reads the place name as a noun, "the vision" (he horasis).

a: if you take wives besides my daughters
p: Some ancient marriage contracts forbade the husband to take another wife. Laban adds the same term.
b: Marriage contracts from Nuzi and from Old Babylonian times sometimes bar the husband from marrying a second wife while the first is living. Laban, who arranged for Jacob to marry two, now forbids any more. It protects his daughters' inheritance and their children's. Bilhah and Zilpah are not counted as wives in this sense.

a: may they judge between us
p: The verb is plural. Laban may be calling on two gods, Abraham's and Nahor's. Jacob swears by his father's God alone.
b: The Hebrew verb yishpetu, "may they judge," is plural, so Laban may be calling on two gods as witnesses, one for each family, as treaties usually did. The Plain English Translation capitalizes "God" all three times, as the Hebrew uses one word, and leaves the question open. "The God of their father" means Terah, who "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). Jacob does not repeat the formula: he swears only by "the Fear of his father Isaac." The Greek and Samaritan texts make the verb singular, and the Greek lacks the last phrase (see the variant on this verse).

a: called his relatives to eat bread
p: Eating together sealed agreements in the ancient world, as with Isaac and Abimelech (26:30).
b: "Bread" means a meal. Sacrifice and a shared meal seal the treaty, as in 26:30 and at Sinai, where Israel's elders "looked upon God, and they ate and drank" (Exodus 24:11). Jacob is the host and offers the sacrifice: he acts as the head of his own clan now.

a: Early in the morning Laban got up
p: In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 32:1, and every verse of chapter 32 is one number higher.
b: The chapter and verse numbers were added long after the text was written. English Bibles, following the Greek and Latin, end chapter 31 with Laban's departure. Hebrew Bibles begin chapter 32 here. So Genesis 32:28 in English is 32:29 in Hebrew. This site uses the English numbering. Laban's farewell is the last we hear of him.

a: angels of God met him
p: Angels met Jacob when he left the land (28:12) and meet him again as he comes back.
b: Jacob saw angels on the stairway at Bethel as he left Canaan (28:12), and now angels meet him as he approaches it again. The two scenes frame his twenty years away. The meeting is told in only two verses and nothing is said, but the point is clear: Jacob is coming back under God's protection, even before he knows how Esau will receive him.

a: Mahanaim
p: Mahanaim means "two camps." God's camp and Jacob's, or Jacob's camp split in two (32:7, 10).
b: Machanayim is a dual form, "two camps." The name may mean God's camp and Jacob's camp side by side. The word machaneh, "camp," then runs through the chapter: Jacob divides his people into "two camps" (32:7–8) and says "now I have become two camps" (32:10). Mahanaim became a town in Gilead, near the Jabbok, where Saul's son Ish-bosheth ruled (2 Samuel 2:8) and David took refuge from Absalom (2 Samuel 17:24). Its exact site is uncertain; Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi on the Jabbok is often proposed.
r: 32:7–10; Joshua 21:38; 2 Samuel 2:8; 2 Samuel 17:24; Song of Songs 6:13

a: Jacob sent messengers
p: The Hebrew word for "angels" in 32:1 and "messengers" here is the same: mal'akhim.
b: Mal'akh means "messenger," human or heavenly. God's mal'akhim come to Jacob (32:1), and Jacob sends his own mal'akhim to Esau. Rashi says Jacob sent real angels; most readers take them as servants. The storyteller sets the two kinds of messengers side by side: heaven's messengers are already with him, while his own go ahead to test the danger. The Greek word angelos has the same double sense.

a: to my lord Esau: 'Your servant Jacob
p: Jacob was blessed as master (27:29), yet he calls Esau "my lord." The rabbis saw a lesson for life under Rome.
b: Isaac's blessing made Jacob "master over your brothers" (27:29, 37), but Jacob now addresses Esau as "my lord" and himself as "your servant," as he will eight times in these chapters. Jewish tradition read this scene as the pattern for Israel's dealings with Edom, meaning Rome. Genesis Rabbah tells that Rabbi Judah the Prince, writing to the emperor, called himself "your servant" and cited this verse. Ramban, however, saw in Jacob's humbling himself a warning: it hints at how the Hasmonean kings brought on their own ruin by seeking an alliance with Rome.

a: four hundred men
p: Four hundred men is a fighting force, the size of David's band in his outlaw years.
b: David's band of outlaws and debtors numbered about four hundred (1 Samuel 22:2; 25:13; 30:10). A man coming to meet his brother with four hundred men is not bringing a welcome party. The messengers do not say what Esau intends, and that silence is what terrifies Jacob. The reader does not learn it either until 33:4.

a: God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac
p: Address, memory of God's word, humility, plea, promise. It is the longest prayer in Genesis.
b: This is the first prayer in the Bible with a full shape, and it has been a model for Jewish and Christian prayer. Jacob addresses God by the covenant names, reminds him of his own command ("Go back," 31:3, 13), confesses his unworthiness, asks plainly for rescue, and ends by holding God to his promise (28:14). Notice what has changed since Bethel: no conditions, no bargain. Readers also note what has not changed: right after he prays, he plans (32:13–21). Many readers see no conflict between praying and planning.

a: I am too small for all the faithful love and all the faithfulness
p: The two great words for God's covenant loyalty: hesed (faithful love) and emet (faithfulness).
b: Chasadim, the plural of hesed, is faithful, loyal love that keeps a commitment; emet is truth, reliability. Together they describe God himself in Exodus 34:6. Jacob confesses he is "too small" (qatonti), a word that also means "younger": the younger son who took the elder's place admits he deserves nothing. The KJV's "I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies" captures the sense.
orig: קָטֹנְתִּי מִכֹּל הַחֲסָדִים וּמִכָּל־הָאֱמֶת (qatonti mikkol hachasadim umikkol ha'emet)

a: thirty nursing camels with their young
p: Over five hundred animals in carefully planned herds. A gift on this scale was tribute.
b: The gift totals 550 animals: 220 goats, 220 sheep, 30 camels with their calves, 50 cattle and 30 donkeys. For the goats and sheep the ratio is one male to ten females; for the cattle one to four, and for the donkeys one to two. These are the kinds of herds a breeder would build. Nursing camels were especially valuable for their milk. Sending the herds one after another, each with the same speech (32:16–20), lets the gift work on Esau again and again before Jacob himself appears.

a: I will cover his face with the gift
p: "Face" appears again and again: cover his face, see his face, lift my face. Then comes Peniel, "face of God."
b: Literally Jacob says: "I will cover his face with the gift that goes before my face, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will lift my face." "Cover" (kipper) is the word later used for atonement, making peace by covering an offense. "Lift the face" means to accept someone, to forgive. The word panim, "face," comes again in 32:21 ("ahead of him," literally "before his face"), in Peniel, "face of God" (32:30), and in 33:10: "seeing your face is like seeing the face of God." Jacob prepares to face his brother and meets God face to face first.
orig: אֲכַפְּרָה פָנָיו (akhapperah fanav); יִשָּׂא פָנָי (yissa fanai)

a: his eleven children
p: Jacob has eleven sons and a daughter, but the Hebrew counts eleven "children." Rashi asks where Dinah was.
b: The Hebrew says "children" (yeladav, as in 33:1–7), yet counts eleven: the sons. Benjamin is not yet born (35:18), so Dinah (30:21) is the missing child, and Rashi asks where she was. Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah, says Jacob shut Dinah in a chest so that Esau would not set eyes on her, and was punished for keeping her from a brother who might have been changed by her, by what happened to her at Shechem (34:2). The midrash is harsh on Jacob here; the plain text may simply be counting heirs.

a: a man wrestled with him
p: Yabboq, Ya'aqov, ye'aveq: river, man and verb all sound alike.
b: The river is the Jabbok (Yabboq), the man is Jacob (Ya'aqov), and the verb "wrestled" is ye'aveq, found only here and in 32:25. It may come from 'avaq, "dust": two men rolling in the dust. The sounds tie the place, the person and the event together. The Jabbok (modern Zarqa River) flows west into the Jordan through a deep gorge in Gilead, and its ford was a border (Numbers 21:24).

a: a man
p: God, an angel, Esau's guardian angel, the Son of God, a river spirit, or Jacob's own soul. Each view has defenders.
b: The text calls him "a man," yet Jacob says he has seen God face to face (32:30), and the man says Jacob has struggled with God (32:28). Hosea 12:3–4 says Jacob "struggled with God ... He struggled against the angel and overcame him." Jewish readers usually say an angel; Genesis Rabbah calls him the guardian prince of Esau, and later tradition names him Samael. Many church fathers, beginning with Justin Martyr, saw the Son of God appearing as a man. Gunkel and other critical scholars traced the story to a folk tale of a river spirit who must leave before dawn. Modern readers also see Jacob wrestling with his past, his brother and his conscience. The text leaves the stranger nameless (32:29).

a: he touched the socket of his hip
p: The thigh stands for strength and offspring. Jacob is blessed and crippled in the same night.
b: The verb naga' means "touch" or "strike"; one touch was enough to put Jacob's hip out of joint, which shows who was really stronger. In Hebrew the thigh (yarekh) stands for strength and for a man's descendants: oaths were sworn with a hand under it (24:2; 47:29), and Jacob's offspring are "those who came out of his thigh" (46:26, literally). Jacob, who always won by his own strength and wits, walks away from his victory limping.

a: because the dawn has come up
t: A night spirit at the river?
p: Gunkel compared the wrestler to river spirits of folklore who lose their power at daybreak.
b: Hermann Gunkel (1901) compared this scene to folktales of a river spirit or night demon who guards a ford, attacks travelers and must vanish before sunrise, and he thought an older story of that kind lies behind it. Many critical scholars still see traces of such a tale in the night setting, the ford and the stranger's hurry to leave. The text itself gives the stranger no name and has Jacob conclude that he has seen God (32:30). Jewish tradition gave its own reason for the dawn: the angel had to go and sing God's praise (Chullin 91b). Traditional readers see no folklore here at all.

a: I will not let you go unless you bless me
p: Hosea says Jacob "wept and pleaded with him for his favor" (Hosea 12:4).
b: Even crippled, Jacob will not let go. All his life he has grabbed for blessing: his brother's heel, the birthright, Isaac's blessing. Now he asks for it openly, from the one who can truly give it. Hosea 12:4 adds a detail Genesis does not: "He wept and pleaded with him for his favor."
