Charles Wesley's hymn "Come, O Thou Traveller Unknown" retells the night from Jacob's side: "I will not let thee go, till I thy name, thy nature know." The "dawn" may be why the stranger must leave: no one may see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20).

a: but Israel
p: The text links it to sarah, "struggle." As a name, it more likely means "God struggles" or "God rules."
b: The narrator explains Israel (Yisra'el) by sarita, "you have struggled." Hebrew names of this shape usually have God (El) as the subject: "Ishmael," "God hears." So scholars suggest "God strives," "God rules" (from sar, prince; the KJV's "as a prince hast thou power"), or "God is upright" (compare Jeshurun, Deuteronomy 32:15). As often in Genesis, the explanation is a pun, not a dictionary. The earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible is on the Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian victory monument from about 1208 BC, which names Israel as a people in Canaan. The name now passes to a nation, and later Christians applied it to the church (Galatians 6:16). The Septuagint reads the last words as a promise: "you were strong with God, and with men you will be mighty."

a: with God and with humans
t: Struggling with God and with people
p: With God at the Jabbok, and with people: Esau, Isaac and Laban.
b: The "humans" Jacob has struggled with are easy to name: Esau, from the womb (25:22), Isaac, whom he deceived, and Laban, who deceived him. The struggle "with God" happened that night, and Jewish readers like Ramban see in it a sign of Israel's history: a people wounded in its struggles but never destroyed. Christian readers have often read Jacob's night as a picture of prayer and of conversion: a self-reliant man who holds on to God and is changed.

a: Why is it that you ask my name?
p: The angel who visits Samson's parents gives the same answer (Judges 13:17–18).
b: In the ancient world knowing a name gave a kind of hold over the one named. Jacob gives his name and is renamed; he asks for the stranger's and is refused. Manoah, Samson's father, asks the angel of the LORD his name and hears, "Why are you asking for my name?... It is wonderful, beyond grasping" (Judges 13:17–18). At the burning bush Moses asks God's name and receives the mysterious "I am who I am" (Exodus 3:13–14). God gives blessing here, not a name.

a: Peniel
p: Peniel means "face of God." To see God's face and live was thought impossible (Exodus 33:20).
b: Peniel (also spelled Penuel, 32:31) means "face of God." Hagar, Gideon and Manoah are all amazed to have seen God or his angel and lived (16:13; Judges 6:22–23; 13:22), and God tells Moses, "You cannot see my face, for no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). John's Gospel says, "Nobody has ever seen God. It is the only one, God, the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known" (John 1:18). Christians who see the wrestler as the Son of God link these verses. Penuel later became a fortified town that Gideon destroyed (Judges 8:8–9, 17) and Jeroboam rebuilt (1 Kings 12:25).

a: he limped because of his hip
p: The sun had set when Jacob fled (28:11). It rises on him as he limps home. Rashi says it rose to heal him.
b: When Jacob left the land, "the sun had gone down" (28:11); now, coming back, "the sun rose on him." The narrator frames Jacob's twenty years between a sunset and a sunrise. Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah, says the sun rose early for his sake, to heal his limp, and links it to Malachi 4:2: "a sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings." Yet the limp remains in the text: the new Israel walks differently from the old Jacob.

a: the people of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh
p: The only food law in Genesis besides the ban on blood (9:4). Jews still observe it.
b: This is the first time the phrase "the people of Israel" (bene Yisra'el) appears, right after the name is given. The gid hanasheh is usually identified with the sciatic nerve and its sinews in the hindquarter. The Mishnah (Chullin 7:1) rules that it is forbidden inside and outside the land of Israel. Removing it takes skill, so in many Jewish communities the hindquarters of kosher animals are simply sold to non-Jews. The law is observed to this day as a memory of Jacob's night.

a: bowed down to the ground seven times
p: Letters to Pharaoh from Canaanite kings in the 1300s BC begin: "At my lord's feet seven times and seven times I fall."
b: The Amarna letters, clay tablets sent to the Egyptian court around 1350 BC by rulers in Canaan and Syria, often open with the formula "at the feet of the king, my lord, seven times and seven times I fall." Jacob greets his brother as a vassal greets an overlord. The scene turns the blessing upside down: Isaac had said "may your mother's sons bow down to you" (27:29), and here the blessed one bows to his mother's son. Jacob also places himself in front of his family, between them and Esau, after sending them ahead the night before.

a: ran to meet him, hugged him, fell on his neck and kissed him
p: Jesus' parable of the lost son uses the same gestures for the father's welcome (Luke 15:20).
b: Esau runs, embraces, falls on his neck and kisses. In the parable of the prodigal son, the father runs, falls on his neck and kisses him (Luke 15:20): the same gestures, though the Greek verbs are not identical and the order differs a little. Joseph's reunions with Benjamin and Jacob use the same gestures (45:14–15; 46:29). Jesus' hearers knew Genesis well, and many scholars think the echo is deliberate. If so, the character who plays the forgiving father is Esau, the one Israel's tradition had come to see as the enemy, and the returning son is Jacob, who had wronged him.

a: kissed him
p: In Hebrew scrolls this word has dots over every letter. Did Esau kiss him sincerely or try to bite him?
b: The Masoretic scribes put dots over the six letters of vayyishshaqehu, "and he kissed him," one of about ten places in the Torah marked this way. The dots probably signaled doubt about the word, but the rabbis read them as a hint. In Genesis Rabbah, Rabbi Simeon ben Eleazar says Esau's kiss was sincere for once; Rabbi Yannai says Esau meant to bite (nashakh) Jacob's neck, but it turned to marble, so "they wept": Jacob for his neck and Esau for his teeth. Rashi cites the saying of Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai: "It is a known rule that Esau hates Jacob, but at that moment his pity was stirred and he kissed him with all his heart."

a: The children with whom God has favored your servant
p: Chanan, "to show grace," with "find favor" (chen) running through the chapter.
b: Jacob credits his children to God's grace (chanan), and in 33:11 his wealth too: "God has been gracious to me." The related noun chen, "favor," comes three times as Jacob tries to "find favor in the eyes of my lord" (33:8, 10, 15). The chapter plays the two together: grace received from God, favor sought from a brother.

a: Last of all Joseph and Rachel came near
p: Jacob lines up his family from least to most loved. Everyone can see it.
b: Slave women and their children first, then Leah and hers, and Rachel and Joseph last, the safest place (33:2). The order is a public ranking, and the narrator repeats it as each group bows. Readers trace the family's later troubles to this favoritism: Joseph's brothers will hate him for being the loved son (37:3–4). Note also that here Joseph comes before his mother, perhaps shielding her.

a: seeing your face is like seeing the face of God
p: After Peniel, Jacob sees God's face in his brother's. Flattery, or the meaning of the whole story?
b: Jacob has just named a place "face of God" (32:30). Now he tells Esau that seeing his face is like seeing God's, "now that you have received me kindly." Some readers hear only the flattery of a nervous man. Others hear the heart of the story: Jacob could not face his brother until he had faced God, and in the brother's forgiveness he meets God's. The same thought is expressed in 1 John 4:20: "the one who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, is not able to love God, whom he has never seen."

a: Please take my blessing
p: Birkhati means "my gift," but it is the word for "blessing." Jacob gives back what he took.
b: Berakhah can mean a gift (1 Samuel 25:27; 2 Kings 5:15), but it is the same word as the "blessing" Jacob took from Esau (27:35–36: "he has taken my blessing"). Many readers see a deliberate return: "take my blessing," Jacob says. Esau had said "I have plenty" (rav, 33:9); Jacob answers "I have everything" (kol). The gift is restitution in all but name.

a: until I come to my lord in Seir
p: Jacob promises to follow to Seir and goes to Succoth instead. Rashi says the promise points to the end of days.
b: Jacob says he will follow at the flock's pace to Seir, and then goes north and west to Succoth and Shechem (33:17–18). Many readers see one last evasion: Jacob is reconciled with Esau but does not trust him. Others think he was right not to bind his household to Esau's war band. Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah, says Jacob was speaking of the messianic age, when "Rescuers will go up on Mount Zion to judge Mount Esau" (Obadiah 21). The brothers meet again only at their father's grave (35:29).

a: That is why the place is named Succoth
p: "Shelters" or "booths." East of the Jordan near the Jabbok, perhaps Tell Deir Alla.
b: Sukkot means "booths, shelters," like the ones Jacob built for his animals. The town lay in the Jordan Valley east of the river (Joshua 13:27; Judges 8:5–16). Many scholars have identified it with Tell Deir Alla, where an inscription about "Balaam son of Beor" was found in 1967, though others place Deir Alla at another biblical town. The name is the same as the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:42–43), but the Bible does not connect this place with the festival.

a: Jacob came safely
p: Shalem means "whole, safe." The KJV and the Greek read it as a place name.
b: The word shalem can be an adjective, "whole, safe and sound," or the name of a town, Salem; the variant on this verse gives the witnesses. Rashi read it as "whole in body, in wealth and in learning." The adjective fits Jacob's vow to "return in peace to my father's house" (28:21), where "in peace" is beshalom. A village called Salim lies a few miles east of Shechem, which keeps the other reading alive.

a: for a hundred qesitahs
t: The second piece of the promised land
p: Abraham bought a grave (ch. 23); Jacob buys a field. Joseph is buried there, and John 4 sets Jesus nearby.
b: The qesitah was some unit of value whose size is unknown (also Joshua 24:32; Job 42:11). The Septuagint and the Vulgate translate "a hundred lambs," perhaps because a coin or weight was marked with or worth a lamb. This is the second land purchase in Canaan, after Abraham's cave at Machpelah (23:16–20). Joseph's bones were later buried on this plot (Joshua 24:32), and John 4:5–6 places Jacob's well "close to the field Jacob gave to Joseph his son," where a Samaritan woman asks Jesus, "Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob? This well was his gift to us" (John 4:12). Jacob later speaks of taking "one shoulder" (shekhem) of land "with my sword and my bow" (48:22). Stephen, retelling history quickly in Acts 7:16, merges this purchase with Abraham's.

a: named it El-Elohe-Israel
p: Or "El is the God of Israel." Jacob uses his new name, and says "my God" at last in his own way.
b: El Elohei Yisra'el can be read "God, the God of Israel" or "El is the God of Israel." El was the name of the high god of the Canaanites, and also the ordinary Hebrew word for God; many scholars think the altar's name claims the land's chief title for the God of Jacob. "Israel" here may mean Jacob himself, newly named: so this fulfills his vow that the LORD would be his God (28:21). The verb "set up" (vayyatsev) is the one used for standing stones, and some scholars think a standing stone stood here originally.

a: went out to look at the daughters of the land
p: Some ancient readers blamed Dinah for "going out." The text puts the guilt on Shechem.
b: Dinah went to visit the women of the region, an ordinary thing to do. Josephus says she went to a festival to see the local women's finery. Genesis Rabbah compares her to her mother, who "went out" to meet Jacob in 30:16, and some later preachers used the verse to warn girls to stay home. Most modern readers, Jewish and Christian, reject that as blaming the victim. The text itself never faults Dinah. Every verb of wrong in 34:2 belongs to Shechem, and the narrator calls what he did "a disgraceful thing" (34:7). Dinah herself never speaks in the chapter.

a: who ruled the region
p: The Hivites were a people of central Canaan. Shechem the man shares the name of the city his family rules.
b: The Hivites appear in the lists of Canaan's peoples (10:17; Exodus 3:8) and lived in the central hills, at Gibeon (Joshua 9:7) and here at Shechem. Shechem the prince has the city's name; his father Hamor's name means "donkey," perhaps from a treaty rite: in texts from Mari, treaties were sealed by killing a donkey, and later the people of Shechem worshiped "Baal of the covenant" (Judges 9:4). The city, at modern Tell Balata near Nablus, was a major walled town in the Middle Bronze Age.

a: He took her and lay with her and dishonored her
p: Took, lay, dishonored. Most read rape here; a few scholars argue the last verb means "shamed," not "forced."
b: The verb 'innah means to humble, degrade, mistreat. It is used of Amnon's rape of his sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13:12, 14, 22), of the gang rape at Gibeah (Judges 19:24; 20:5), and of taking a captive woman (Deuteronomy 21:14). "Lay with her" is literally "laid her," with a direct object rather than the usual "with her," which many take as a sign of force. Most translations and commentators (for example Sternberg and Wenham) read rape. Lyn Bechtel (1994) and Ellen van Wolde (2002) argued that 'innah marks a loss of status, sex outside proper marriage arrangements, and does not in itself say there was force. Either way, Dinah had no say, and her brothers call it treating her "like a prostitute" (34:31).
orig: וַיִּקַּח אֹתָהּ וַיִּשְׁכַּב אֹתָהּ וַיְעַנֶּהָ (vayyiqqach otah vayyishkav otah vay'anneha)

a: spoke to the girl's heart
p: Shechem "loved" her and "spoke to her heart," but he also keeps her in his house (34:26).
b: "Speaking to the heart" means comforting or wooing (50:21; Judges 19:3; Hosea 2:14; Isaiah 40:2). Unlike Amnon, who hated Tamar after he raped her (2 Samuel 13:15), Shechem wants to marry Dinah. Some readers find in this a partial redemption of Shechem. Others note how familiar the pattern is: the man acts first, then speaks of love, and the woman's wishes are never asked. Dinah is in Shechem's house when her brothers arrive (34:26), so the text implies she was held there throughout the negotiations.

a: Get me this girl as my wife
p: Shechem asks his father to arrange the marriage, as Samson did (Judges 14:2). Dinah's father is never asked first.
b: In Israel and its neighbors, marriages were arranged between families: the groom's father approached the bride's father, and a bride price was agreed (24:1–53; Judges 14:2). Shechem reverses the order. He takes Dinah first and arranges the marriage afterward. The word he uses, yaldah, "girl," suggests Dinah was young; by Genesis' timeline she was probably in her early or middle teens.

a: he had defiled Dinah his daughter
p: Timme', "made unclean," is the word of purity laws. The narrator uses it three times (34:5, 13, 27).
b: To "defile" (timme') is to make ritually unclean, a word mostly used in the laws of purity (Leviticus 15:31) and of sexual sin (Leviticus 18:20; Numbers 5:13; Ezekiel 18:6). Using it for Dinah shows how the family saw the act: not only an injury to her but a stain on the family's holiness. The chapter's other repeated words, "disgrace" (34:7, 14) and "daughter" or "sister," keep the family's honor in view.

a: so Jacob kept quiet until they came
p: Jacob says nothing when his daughter is violated. His only later words are about his own safety (34:30).
b: Jacob "kept quiet" (hecherish). Readers explain it differently: caution, a father waiting for the clan's men before acting, or indifference toward Leah's daughter. The story offers no warm word from him to Dinah or about her. When he finally speaks, it is to complain that his sons have endangered him (34:30). Only on his deathbed does he condemn the violence of Simeon and Levi (49:5–7). The contrast with David, who "was very angry" but did nothing when Tamar was raped (2 Samuel 13:21), is often drawn.

a: a disgraceful thing in Israel
t: "Such a thing is not done in Israel"
p: Tamar uses almost the same words to Amnon (2 Samuel 13:12). The two stories echo each other.
b: Nevalah is an outrage against the moral order, especially sexual: the girl who hides her lost virginity (Deuteronomy 22:21), the crime at Gibeah (Judges 19:23; 20:6, 10), Achan's sin (Joshua 7:15). When Amnon seizes Tamar she pleads, "Such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing" (2 Samuel 13:12). In Genesis, "in Israel" is surprising, since the nation does not yet exist; critical scholars see the later writer's world showing through, and traditional readers note that Jacob has just been named Israel (32:28). Both stories have a sister violated, a passive father and a brother's bloody revenge.

a: Make the bride price and gift as high as you like
p: Israel's law says a man who seduces or rapes an unbetrothed virgin must pay the bride price and marry her.
b: Exodus 22:16–17 says a man who seduces an unengaged virgin must pay the bride price (mohar) and marry her, unless her father refuses. Deuteronomy 22:28–29 says a man who seizes an unengaged virgin must pay fifty shekels and marry her, and may never divorce her. Shechem's offer is exactly that legal remedy. To modern readers such laws, which make a victim marry her attacker, are deeply troubling; ancient readers saw them as protecting a woman who would otherwise be unmarriageable. Dinah's brothers refuse the remedy and choose blood instead.

a: with trickery
p: Bemirmah, "with deceit": the same word as Jacob's trick on Isaac (27:35).
b: Mirmah was the word for Jacob's theft of the blessing (27:35), and Laban's trick was rimmah (29:25). Now Jacob's sons use trickery, but against outsiders and with a sword behind it. The narrator adds at once why: "because he had defiled Dinah their sister." The reader is given their motive and left to judge the means.

a: a man who has a foreskin
p: The sign of God's covenant (17:10–14) becomes a trap. A "disgrace" (cherpah) is the word Joshua uses of uncircumcision.
b: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (17:10–14), open to any male of the household, including foreigners (17:12–13). The brothers offer it as a path to becoming "one people" (34:16) while planning to use the men's pain to kill them. Cherpah, "disgrace," is the word Joshua uses when Israel is circumcised at Gilgal: "Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt" (Joshua 5:9). Readers across traditions have seen this abuse of a holy sign as part of the crime.

a: Their livestock, their goods and all their animals, will they not be ours?
p: Hamor tells Jacob "The land will lie open before you" (34:10) and tells his own people "their goods will be ours."
b: To Jacob's family Hamor offered land and trade (34:10). To his own townsmen he leaves out Dinah and the love story and says that Jacob's wealth will end up theirs. He also leaves out who asked for circumcision. So the chapter shows two families bargaining in bad faith: the brothers plan murder, the Shechemites plan absorption. Neither side is innocent of greed, though the brothers' deceit is far bloodier.

a: All who went out of the city gate
p: "Those who go out of the gate" are the town's men of full standing, the ones who go out to war and to council.
b: The phrase, repeated twice in the verse, means the citizens who come and go through the gate, where business and justice were done (34:20; Ruth 4:1). These are the fighting men. Every one of them agrees, which shows Hamor's and Shechem's authority. It also means every man of fighting age is disabled three days later.

a: while they were in pain
p: Pain after circumcision was thought worst on the third day. The Talmud uses this verse in a Sabbath law.
b: The Mishnah (Shabbat 19:3) cites this verse to rule that a baby circumcised on the third day before the Sabbath may be bathed even on the Sabbath, because the third day is the most dangerous. Simeon and Levi, Leah's second and third sons and Dinah's full brothers, strike then. Jacob later curses their anger and scatters their tribes (49:5–7). Simeon was absorbed into Judah (Joshua 19:1–9), and Levi received no land, though its zeal was later turned to God's service (Exodus 32:26–29; Numbers 25:6–13).

a: while it felt secure
p: Betach can describe the city (unsuspecting) or the attackers (confident). The KJV has "boldly."
b: Betach means "in safety, with confidence." The KJV, following some older interpreters, applies it to Simeon and Levi: they came "boldly." Most modern versions apply it to the city: they attacked a town that thought itself safe (compare Judges 18:7, 27; Ezekiel 38:11). Either way, the attack depended on the men being helpless.

a: all their little children and their wives they carried off as captives
p: The women of Shechem, who had done nothing, are taken captive. The story does not hide it.
b: The revenge for one woman's violation ends with every woman and child of the city taken as plunder. Many readers, ancient and modern, have noted the irony: the brothers punish the treatment of their sister by seizing other men's wives and daughters. The narrator lists it without comment, as Hebrew narrative often does, and lets Jacob's later curse speak: "their blades are tools of violence" (49:5).

a: You have made me stink
t: "You have stirred up trouble for me"
p: "Make me stink" (hiv'ishani) means "made me hated." "Trouble" ('akhar) is the word behind the Valley of Achor.
b: Hiv'ishani, "you have made me stink," is a vivid idiom for "made me hateful" (Exodus 5:21; 1 Samuel 13:4; 2 Samuel 10:6). 'Akhar, "to bring disaster," is used of Achan, "the troubler of Israel," whose valley is named Achor (Joshua 7:25–26; 1 Kings 18:17–18). Jacob's protest is about danger, not justice, and he speaks of "me" again and again. Many readers fault him for it. On his deathbed he speaks instead of a "shoulder" of land (shekhem) he took "with my sword and my bow" (48:22), which some read as Shechem; others think a leader with "only a few men" (literally "men of number") was right to fear.

a: Like a prostitute, is that how he should treat our sister?
p: The chapter ends with the brothers' question and no verdict. Interpreters have argued about it ever since.
b: The narrator does not say who was right. Meir Sternberg argued that the story is built to make readers side with the brothers' outrage, while still judging their deceit. Danna Fewell and David Gunn (1991) replied that it equally exposes their violence and their treating Dinah as family property. Jewish tradition is divided: Maimonides held the men of Shechem deserved death for failing to bring Shechem to justice, while Ramban rejected this and pointed to Jacob's curse (49:5–7). The Book of Jubilees (chapter 30), Judith 9:2–4 and the Testament of Levi praise the brothers' zeal. Many Christian readers see in the chapter what happens when God's people answer evil with evil.

a: go up to Bethel
p: God sends Jacob back to the place of his vow (28:20–22). The circle of Jacob's journey closes.
b: God reminds Jacob of the day he ran from Esau and of the vow he made then (28:20–22; 31:13). The command comes right after the disaster at Shechem, and it rescues the family from a dangerous place (34:30). "Go up" is the usual verb for going to a holy place, which is why later pilgrim psalms are "songs of going up" (Psalms 120–134).

a: Put away the foreign gods in your midst
p: Joshua later calls Israel to the same thing, at the same place: Shechem (Joshua 24:14–26).
b: Jacob's household had idols: Rachel's stolen household gods (31:19), and perhaps images taken with the plunder of Shechem (34:29). Before meeting God they wash and change clothes, as Israel will before Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14). At Shechem, Joshua later tells Israel to "put away the foreign gods that are among you" and sets up a stone "under the oak" there (Joshua 24:23, 26). Many scholars think both texts reflect a covenant ceremony held at Shechem. Traditional readers see Joshua consciously repeating Jacob's act.

a: the rings in their ears
p: Earrings were often amulets carrying images or charms. Aaron made the golden calf from earrings (Exodus 32:2–4).
b: In the ancient Near East earrings were often amulets, sometimes shaped like or engraved with gods. They are given up with the idols, as part of the same religion. Aaron made the golden calf from Israel's gold earrings (Exodus 32:2–4), and Gideon's ephod was made from captured earrings (Judges 8:24–27). Hosea pictures Israel decking herself with rings to go after the Baals (Hosea 2:13).

a: the oak that is by Shechem
p: Abraham first camped at "the oak of Moreh" at Shechem (12:6). It was a holy tree for centuries.
b: The great tree at Shechem was a landmark: Abraham's first stop in Canaan was "the oak of Moreh" ("oak of the teacher," perhaps where oracles were given, 12:6). Joshua set up a covenant stone "under the oak" there (Joshua 24:26), and Abimelech was made king "by the oak of the pillar at Shechem" (Judges 9:6). Jacob buries the idols in the very ground of the promised land, and the family leaves them behind.

a: a terror from God
p: Jacob feared revenge (34:30). God sends a terror on the cities so that no one pursues.
b: Jacob feared the Canaanites would wipe him out (34:30). Instead a chittat Elohim, "terror from God" or "a great terror," falls on the surrounding towns. The same protection is promised to Israel entering the land (Exodus 23:27; Deuteronomy 2:25). The story does not say the family deserved it: God keeps his promise of 28:15 in spite of them.

a: God had revealed himself to him
p: The verb is plural: "God (Elohim) revealed themselves." Grammar of majesty, or the angels of 28:12?
b: Elohim, "God," is plural in form but almost always takes a singular verb. Here the verb niglu, "revealed," is plural, as in 20:13 and 2 Samuel 7:23. Some take it as a grammar of majesty or as old usage; others think it refers to the angels Jacob saw on the stairway (28:12), since elohim can mean heavenly beings. Some older Christian writers saw a hint of the Trinity; most scholars today, Christian and Jewish, do not read it that way. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint and the Vulgate all have a singular verb (see the variant on this verse).

a: Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died
p: Why mention a nurse? The rabbis heard a hidden notice of Rebekah's own death.
b: Rebekah's nurse went with her from Haran (24:59) but is named only here, at her death. Allon-bacuth means "Oak of Weeping." Rashi, citing Genesis Rabbah, says Jacob received news of his mother's death at the same place, and that allon sounds like the Greek allon, "another": a second weeping. Genesis never tells of Rebekah's death, perhaps, the midrash suggests, so that people would not curse the womb that bore Esau. We learn only that she was buried at Machpelah (49:31). Jacob never saw his mother again.

a: Israel will be your name
p: Jacob was already named Israel at the Jabbok (32:28). Why again, at Bethel?
b: Critical scholars usually see two traditions: the Jabbok story (often assigned to J) and a Priestly version (P), in which God renames Jacob at Bethel without a struggle, as he renamed Abraham (17:5). Traditional readers see a confirmation: the name given by the night wrestler is now given by God in daylight at the place of the vow. Unlike Abraham, Jacob keeps being called Jacob, often in the same verse as Israel (46:2). The Talmud (Berakhot 13a) notes the difference: it is wrong to call Abraham "Abram," but Jacob is still called Jacob, because the new name was added, not substituted.

a: kings will come out of your loins
p: The promise of kings, first made to Abraham and Sarah (17:6, 16), now passes to Jacob.
b: God repeats to Jacob what he told Abraham: "Be fruitful and multiply," the command of creation (1:28; 9:1), with nations and kings among his descendants (17:6, 16). Israel's kings came from Jacob's sons: Saul from Benjamin, who is born in this chapter, and David from Judah. "A gathering of nations" is later linked to Ephraim and Manasseh (48:4, 19). Christians read the promise of kings as reaching its height in Jesus, "son of David" (Matthew 1:1).

a: He poured a drink offering on it
p: Jacob sets up a stone, anoints it and names Bethel, all things he did in 28:18–19.
b: This is the first drink offering (nesekh) in the Bible: wine poured out to God, later part of regular worship (Exodus 29:40; Numbers 15:5). Jacob also sets up a stone, pours oil and names the place Bethel, repeating 28:18–19. Critical scholars see a Priestly retelling of the Bethel founding; traditional readers see Jacob renewing the vow on his return, as he promised (28:21–22). The repetition also completes Jacob's story: what began as a dream in flight ends as worship in the land.

a: some distance
p: Kivrat ha'arets is a measure of distance no one can now define.
b: Kivrat ha'arets, perhaps "a stretch of land," appears only here, in 48:7 and in 2 Kings 5:19. It means a short but real distance. The ancient translators did not know it either: the Septuagint simply copies it as a name, Chabratha. The Greek also begins this verse with the line the Hebrew has at 35:21, about the tower of Gader (Migdal-eder); see the variant on this verse.

a: This one too is a son for you
p: Rachel had prayed, "May the LORD add another son" (30:24). The midwife's words tell her the prayer is answered.
b: When Joseph was born, Rachel named him "May he add," asking for another son (30:24). The midwife's comfort is that God has said yes. It is a cruel fulfillment: Rachel, who once cried "Give me children! If you don't, I am a dead woman" (30:1), dies giving birth to the second. The midwife's "Do not be afraid" is said to Phinehas's wife in the same situation (1 Samuel 4:20).

a: Ben-oni
t: Son of my sorrow, son of the right hand
p: Rachel names him Ben-oni, probably "son of my sorrow." Jacob renames him Benjamin, "son of the right hand."
b: Ben-oni may mean "son of my sorrow" ('oni, "trouble, mourning") or "son of my strength" ('on, as in 49:3, where Reuben is "the first of my strength"). Most take it as "sorrow," a mother's dying cry. Jacob will not leave his son with that name. Binyamin means "son of the right hand," the side of strength and favor (Psalm 110:1), or "son of the south," since the right hand faces south when one faces east. Texts from Mari on the Euphrates (1700s BC) mention a tribal group called "sons of the right" or "southerners." Benjamin is the only one of Jacob's sons born in Canaan.

a: which is Bethlehem
p: This verse puts it near Bethlehem. 1 Samuel 10:2 seems to place it north of Jerusalem in Benjamin.
b: Two traditions stand side by side. Here and in 48:7, Rachel is buried "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem," south of Jerusalem, where the traditional Rachel's Tomb stands today. But Samuel tells Saul he will pass "Rachel's grave in Benjamin's territory, at Zelzah" (1 Samuel 10:2), north of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping at Ramah, also in Benjamin (Jeremiah 31:15). Many scholars think there was an Ephrathah in Benjamin too (compare 1 Chronicles 2:50–51) and that "which is Bethlehem" is a later explanation linking it to the better-known Ephrathah of Judah (Ruth 4:11; Micah 5:2). Others accept the Bethlehem site and read 1 Samuel 10:2 differently.

a: It is the standing stone of Rachel's grave to this day
p: Rashi: Jacob buried her by the road so she could weep for her children as they passed into exile.
b: Rachel is the only matriarch not buried at Machpelah. Rashi (on 48:7) says Jacob buried her on the road by God's command, so that when the exiles were led past toward Babylon she would weep and pray for them, as Jeremiah says: "Rachel crying over her children ... Stop your voice from weeping and your eyes from shedding tears, for your work will be paid" (Jeremiah 31:15–16). Matthew applies Jeremiah's words to the murdered children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18). The present building at the traditional site was restored by Moses Montefiore in 1841 and remains a place of prayer, especially for women longing for children.

a: Migdal-eder
p: Micah 4:8 speaks of a "tower of the flock." A Targum says the Messiah will appear there.
b: Migdal 'eder means "tower of the flock," a watchtower for shepherds. Micah 4:8 calls Jerusalem "tower of the flock, hill of daughter Zion," just before his prophecy of a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says Migdal-eder is "the place from which the King Messiah will be revealed at the end of days." A popular Christian claim says the shepherds of Luke 2:8 kept temple sacrificial lambs there. That is built on one line of the Mishnah (Shekalim 7:4) about animals found between Jerusalem and Migdal-eder, and the details are speculation.

a: Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine
p: A son taking his father's concubine claimed his place. Reuben loses the firstborn's rights (49:3–4).
b: Taking a ruler's concubine was a bid for his power: Absalom did it publicly to David (2 Samuel 16:21–22), and Adonijah's request for David's attendant Abishag cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13–25). Jacob says nothing now, but on his deathbed he strips Reuben of his rank (49:3–4; 1 Chronicles 5:1). The Talmud (Shabbat 55b) says, "Whoever says Reuben sinned is mistaken": he only moved his father's bed from Bilhah's tent to Leah's after Rachel died. The Mishnah (Megillah 4:10) lists this verse among passages read in the synagogue but not translated aloud. Hebrew manuscripts also leave a blank space in the middle of the verse.

a: Now the sons of Jacob were twelve
p: With Benjamin born, the twelve are complete: the ancestors of Israel's twelve tribes.
b: The list arranges the sons by mother, not by birth order: Leah's six, Rachel's two, then Bilhah's and Zilpah's. Twelve became the number of Israel: twelve stones in the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:21), twelve stones from the Jordan (Joshua 4:8), twelve apostles who will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), and the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12).

a: born to him in Paddan-aram
p: Benjamin was born in Canaan (35:16–18), yet he is in a list of sons born in Paddan-aram.
b: The closing line says all these sons were born in Paddan-aram, though the chapter has just told Benjamin's birth near Bethlehem. Hebrew summaries often speak of the group as a whole without stopping for exceptions; 46:15 counts Dinah among Leah's "sons." Critical scholars see the hand of the Priestly writer, who supplies such lists. Either way, readers should not press the line as an error-proof census.

a: a hundred and eighty years
t: Isaac's long life and the story's order
p: By the numbers, Isaac was still alive when Joseph was sold. The narrator closes his story early.
b: Isaac was 60 when the twins were born (25:26), so Jacob was 120 when Isaac died. Jacob was 130 when he met Pharaoh (47:9), and Joseph was then about 39 (41:46; 45:6). So Joseph was sold at 17 (37:2) when Jacob was about 108, twelve years before Isaac's death. Genesis finishes Isaac's story before beginning Joseph's, as it finished Terah's (11:32) and Abraham's (25:7–8) before going on. Long lifespans are taken literally by traditional readers; others read them as honorific or symbolic numbers.

a: his sons Esau and Jacob buried him
p: As Isaac and Ishmael buried Abraham (25:9), the rival twins stand together at their father's burial.
b: Abraham's two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, met at his grave (25:9); now Isaac's twin sons do the same. Esau is named first, the firstborn by birth. The burial is at the cave of Machpelah near Hebron (49:31). The two will not meet again in the story. To be "gathered to his people" means to join one's ancestors in death (25:8; 49:33). "Old and satisfied with days" describes a full life (Job 42:17).

a: This is the family history of Esau
p: The tenth of Genesis' eleven headings, "these are the generations of." Esau's comes twice (36:1, 9).
b: Genesis is organized by the formula elleh toledot, "these are the generations of," rendered "family history" throughout this translation, which appears at 2:4, 5:1, 6:9, 10:1, 11:10, 11:27, 25:12, 25:19, 36:1, 36:9 and 37:2. The pattern is steady: the line that is not chosen is dealt with briefly (Ishmael in 25:12–18, Esau here), and then the story returns to the chosen line at length (Isaac in 25:19, Jacob in 37:2). The brief list does not mean Esau is forgotten: Deuteronomy 2:5 says God gave Seir to Esau as his own possession.

a: that is, Edom
p: The red land south and east of the Dead Sea. Its kingdom, copper mines and capital Bozrah are known from archaeology.
b: Edom means "red," for Esau's ruddy skin and the red stew (25:25, 30), and for the red sandstone of its mountains. It lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea, on both sides of the Arabah valley. An Egyptian papyrus from the late 1200s BC (Papyrus Anastasi VI) mentions Shasu nomads "of Edom" being let through a border fort. Excavations at the copper mines of Faynan (Khirbat en-Nahas) show large-scale, organized production in the 1000s and 900s BC, which some archaeologists (Thomas Levy, Erez Ben-Yosef) link to an early Edomite power. The walled capital at Bozrah (Busayra) dates mainly from the 700s to 500s BC. Scholars still debate how early a true kingdom existed.

a: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite
p: The names of Esau's wives differ in 26:34, 28:9 and here. Many explanations have been offered.
b: In 26:34 and 28:9 Esau's wives are Judith daughter of Beeri, Basemath daughter of Elon, and Mahalath daughter of Ishmael. In 36:2–3 they are Adah daughter of Elon, Oholibamah daughter of Anah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael. Rashi and other harmonizers say the women had two names each: Basemath ("fragrance") was a nickname for Mahalath, and Judith was renamed Oholibamah. Most critical scholars think chapter 36 draws on a separate Edomite list of clans, whose names did not match the family stories. The overlap of names (Basemath appears in both lists, for different women) suggests the traditions were already mixed before Genesis was finished.

a: he went to a land away from Jacob his brother
p: The Hebrew says "to a land" with no name, which is odd. Some ancient translations fill one in.
b: The Hebrew reads literally "he went to a land from the face of Jacob his brother." A place name such as Seir seems to be missing, and ancient translations fill the gap in different ways (see the variant on this verse). The verse also seems to conflict with 32:3, where Esau already lives in Seir. Harmonizers suggest Esau had a base in Seir earlier and moved there fully only now. Critical scholars usually assign 36:6–8 to the Priestly writer, who tells the brothers' parting as a peaceful split over pasture, like Abraham and Lot (13:6).

a: The land where they were living as foreigners could not carry them both
p: Almost the same words describe Abraham and Lot's parting in 13:6.
b: "The land could not carry the two of them" (13:6) explained why Abraham and Lot separated; now the same reason sends Esau away. In both cases the chosen heir stays in Canaan, and the other goes to the east or south and becomes the father of a neighboring nation (Moab and Ammon from Lot, 19:37–38; Edom from Esau). The quiet ending contrasts with the threat of murder in 27:41.

a: Teman
p: Teman became a name for Edom's land. Kenaz is linked to Caleb, a hero of Judah.
b: Teman was a region of Edom famous for wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 9), and Job's friend Eliphaz is "the Temanite" (Job 2:11), with the same name as Esau's son. "God came from Teman," says Habakkuk 3:3. Kenaz's descendants, the Kenizzites, include Caleb son of Jephunneh (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6) and Othniel son of Kenaz, Israel's first judge (Judges 3:9). So Edomite clans were absorbed into Judah, and the border between the brothers' peoples was never sealed.
r: Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 1:9; Job 2:11; Habakkuk 3:3; Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6; Judges 3:9

a: she bore Amalek to Eliphaz
p: Amalek, Israel's bitterest enemy, descends from Esau. The Talmud says it happened because the family rejected Timna.
b: The Amalekites attacked Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 17:8–16) and became the enemy Israel was told to remember and blot out (Deuteronomy 25:17–19; 1 Samuel 15). Haman "the Agagite" in Esther is understood as a descendant of Amalek's king Agag (Esther 3:1; 1 Samuel 15:8). The Talmud (Sanhedrin 99b) tells that Timna, a princess (36:22), wanted to join Abraham's family; Abraham, Isaac and Jacob turned her away, so she became the concubine of Esau's son, saying "better a servant to this people than a princess of another." Amalek came from her, and the Talmud concludes, "They should not have pushed her away."

a: clan chiefs
p: The KJV's "dukes" comes from Latin dux, "leader." The Hebrew alluf means a clan chief.
b: Alluf is a tribal chief, the head of a clan. It may be related to 'elef, "thousand," also used for a clan unit (Judges 6:15; Micah 5:2). The KJV's "duke" followed the Latin dux, which in 1611 still meant simply "leader," not a European noble. Moses' Song mentions "the chiefs of Edom" trembling at the Exodus (Exodus 15:15). Several names here are also place names in Edom (Teman, Kenaz), so the list may be a map of clans as much as a family tree.

a: Seir the Horite
p: The earlier people of Seir: "cave dwellers," Hurrians, or simply natives of the land?
b: Deuteronomy says the Horites lived in Seir before the descendants of Esau destroyed them and settled in their place (Deuteronomy 2:12, 22). The name was long explained from chor, "cave," as cave dwellers, which fits the rock-cut landscape of the region. In the 1900s many scholars identified them with the Hurrians, a people of northern Mesopotamia and Syria well known from Nuzi and Mitanni. But the Horite names here are Semitic, not Hurrian, so many now think the biblical Horites were simply the native people of Seir. The list shows Esau's family marrying into them (36:2, 25).

a: the hot springs
p: Yemim appears only here. The KJV has "mules," the Latin Vulgate "hot waters."
b: Nobody is sure what Anah found. The Latin Vulgate has aquas calidas, "hot waters," and there are hot springs east of the Dead Sea (Callirrhoe, at Zarqa Ma'in). The KJV's "mules" follows a rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Pesachim 54a) that Anah crossbred donkeys and horses, which fits his tending donkeys. Targum Onqelos reads "mighty men," perhaps thinking of the Emim, an ancient giant people of the region (Deuteronomy 2:10–11). The Septuagint simply copies the word as a name, Iamin. Most modern versions follow the Vulgate.

a: These are the sons of Dishon
p: The Hebrew here spells the name like Dishan, but the context and 1 Chronicles 1:41 show Dishon is meant.
b: The two Horite chiefs Dishon and Dishan have names that differ by one vowel letter. In this verse the Hebrew spelling matches Dishan, but the sons listed belong to Dishon son of Anah (36:25), as 1 Chronicles 1:41 shows, and most translations print Dishon. The Plain English Translation does too; see the variant on this verse. The same parallel list spells "Hemdan" as "Hamran": in Hebrew script the letters for d and r look almost alike, a common cause of name differences between Genesis and Chronicles.
orig: דִּישָׁן / דִּישׁוֹן (Dishan / Dishon); חֶמְדָּן / חַמְרָן (Hemdan / Hamran)

a: before any king reigned over the people of Israel
t: Who wrote this verse, and when?
p: This line seems written after Israel had kings. It became famous in debates over who wrote the Torah.
b: The verse looks back from a time when Israel had a king, at least Saul (about 1020 BC). Abraham ibn Ezra (1100s) mentions a scholar named Yitzhaki who said the list was written in King Jehoshaphat's day, and rejects him sharply: "his book deserves to be burned." Spinoza (1670) cited this verse as evidence that Moses did not write the whole Torah. Critical scholars agree that the list comes from the monarchy period or later. Traditional answers include: Moses wrote it as prophecy (compare the promise of kings in 35:11 and the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14–20); a later inspired editor added it; or the "king" meant is Moses himself, called "king in Jeshurun" (Deuteronomy 33:5).

a: Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom
p: No king is the son of the one before. Each comes from a different town, perhaps chosen or seized power.
b: The eight kings in 36:32–39 never succeed father to son, and each has a different home town. Some scholars think Edom's kingship was elective or tribal; others think the list joins rulers of different regions into one sequence. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan identifies Bela son of Beor with Balaam son of Beor (Numbers 22:5), a link many modern readers also notice, though most think the names are simply alike. Dinhabah, the city, is unknown.

a: Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah
p: An appendix in the Greek Job identifies Job with Jobab, king of Edom. Bozrah was Edom's capital.
b: The Septuagint adds a note at the end of Job (42:17) saying Job "was formerly called Jobab" and ruled in Edom, descended from Esau. The idea links Job's land of Uz (Job 1:1; compare Uz in Genesis 36:28 and Lamentations 4:21, "Edom ... in the land of Uz") with Edom. Bozrah (modern Busayra) was Edom's main city, excavated by Crystal-M. Bennett in the 1970s. Isaiah pictures God coming from Bozrah with garments stained red (Isaiah 63:1), and Amos says fire will devour its strongholds (Amos 1:12).
r: Job 1:1; Job 42:17; 36:28; Lamentations 4:21; Isaiah 34:6; Isaiah 63:1; Amos 1:12

a: who struck down Midian in the country of Moab
p: One of the few details of a king's deeds in the list. It may come from an Edomite record.
b: Midian, a people of the desert east and south of Edom, appears as Israel's enemy in Numbers 25 and Judges 6–8, and Moab lay north of Edom. A battle between Edom and Midian on Moab's land is otherwise unknown. Such brief notes suggest the writer used a real king list from Edom. Another Hadad, an Edomite prince, later fled to Egypt from David's army and returned to trouble Solomon (1 Kings 11:14–22).

a: Rehoboth on the River
p: "The River" usually means the Euphrates, far from Edom. Here it may be a local stream.
b: In the Bible "the River" with no name normally means the Euphrates (31:21). A king of Edom from the Euphrates is possible but unlikely. Many scholars think a local river or wadi of Edom is meant, or a town such as Rehoboth-Ir. The name Shaul is the same as Israel's first king Saul.

a: This is Esau, the father of Edom
p: Edom's story continues: enemy of Judah, then forced into Judaism, then Herod. In rabbinic thought Edom became Rome.
b: Edom and Judah fought for centuries (2 Kings 8:20–22; 14:7), and the prophets condemn Edom for joining in Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7). Edomites moved into southern Judah, called Idumea in Greek times. The Hasmonean king John Hyrcanus conquered them about 125 BC and made them accept circumcision (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258). Herod the Great was an Idumean. The rabbis then used "Edom" as a code name for Rome, and later for Christian Rome, so that the twins' rivalry became a picture of Israel and the empire. Malachi 1:2–4 and Romans 9:13 stand behind Christian readings of the same rivalry.
r: 2 Kings 8:20–22; Obadiah 1:10–14; Psalm 137:7; Malachi 1:2–4; Romans 9:13; Mark 3:8
